chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Somebody must have spread lies about Josef K.: one morning he was taken into custody, although he had done nothing wrong. His landlady, Mrs Grubach, employed a cook who brought him breakfast at roughly eight each morning; today she failed to appear. Nothing of the kind had ever happened. For a little while K. waited, watching from his pillow the old woman who lived across the way and was observing him with a curiosity quite foreign to her habits; then, puzzled and hungry together, he rang. A knock came at once, and in stepped somebody he had never encountered in this flat. Slim but solidly built, the man wore close-fitting black clothes furnished, rather like a travelling suit, with assorted pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons and a belt, which gave them an unusually serviceable appearance, though their particular purpose remained obscure. “Who might you be?” K. asked, already half sitting up. Ignoring the question, apparently expecting his presence to be accepted without inquiry, the man confined himself to asking: “Was it you who rang?” K. replied, “Anna is to bring me breakfast,” and for the time being tried to work out who this man actually was by silently observing him and thinking it over. But the stranger did not submit to scrutiny for long. Turning, he opened the door a fraction and told someone evidently just outside it: “He wants Anna to bring him breakfast.” A little laughter sounded from the adjoining room; one could not tell from its sound whether several people were laughing. Although this could have told the stranger nothing he had not known already, he now announced to K., as if delivering a report: “That cannot be done.” “That is a new development,” K. said, springing out of bed and hurriedly pulling on his trousers. “Let me see who these people next door are, and how Mrs Grubach proposes to answer for my being disturbed.” It immediately occurred to him that he need not have said this aloud, and that in saying it he had in a sense conceded the stranger's right to supervise him; just now, however, that scarcely seemed to matter. The stranger did take it that way, for he said: “Wouldn't staying here be better?” “I have no wish to stay here, or to be addressed by you until you have introduced yourself.” “I meant well,” the stranger said, opening the door now of his own accord. K. entered the adjoining room more slowly than he intended. At first sight it looked almost precisely as it had the previous evening. This was Mrs Grubach's sitting room; among its abundance of furniture, covers, china and photographs there was perhaps a little more space today than usual, but that was not immediately apparent, particularly since the chief alteration was a man seated with a book beside the open window, who now glanced up. “Your room was where you should have stayed! Didn't Franz tell you?” “Well, what is it you want?” K. asked, looking from this new acquaintance to the man called Franz, who had stopped in the doorway, and then back again. Through the open window the old woman could be seen once more. With a truly aged person's inquisitiveness she had moved to the window now facing them so as to miss nothing. “I only want Mrs Grubach—” K. said, making a movement as if to break away from the two men, although neither was anywhere near him, and preparing to go on. “No,” said the one by the window, tossing his book onto a small table and getting up. “Leaving is not permitted. You are in custody, after all.” “So it would appear,” K. replied; then he asked: “And on what grounds?” “Explaining that is outside our assignment. Return to your room and wait there. Proceedings have been set in motion, and in due course you will be informed of everything. In speaking to you so kindly I am already exceeding my instructions. Still, I hope nobody but Franz can hear me, and he too is treating you kindly against every regulation. If your luck holds as well as it did when your guards were chosen, you have grounds for confidence.” K. wanted to sit, but now discovered that the armchair at the window was the only seat anywhere in the room. “You'll come to recognise the truth of all this,” Franz said, approaching him together with the other man. That second man in particular towered well above K. and repeatedly patted his shoulder. Both examined K.'s nightshirt. They said he would now have to put on a far inferior shirt, but that they would keep this one, together with his other linen, and restore it to him if his business turned out favourably. “Better to entrust your belongings to us than to the store,” they said, “because things are often misappropriated there; besides, once a certain time has passed everything is sold, whether the proceedings concerned have ended or not. And cases of this sort go on for so long, especially lately. You would eventually receive the proceeds from the store, of course, but in the first place the proceeds are small to begin with: a sale is decided by the size of the bribe, not the size of the bid; and experience shows that sums like these shrink further as they are passed from one hand to another and carried over year after year.” K. scarcely attended to their speeches. Whatever control over his possessions he might still retain meant little to him; what mattered much more was getting a clear understanding of his situation. In these people's presence he could not even think. The second guard's belly—for guards were the only thing they could be—kept bumping him, almost companionably; yet whenever he raised his eyes he saw, wholly at odds with this fat body, a lean, bony face with a prominent nose turned sideways, communicating over his head with the other guard. Who could these people be? What were they talking about? Which authority employed them? Surely he lived under the rule of law; peace prevailed everywhere, every statute remained in force; who dared invade his lodgings? His usual inclination was to take things as lightly as possible, to believe in the worst only once it had happened, and to make no provision for the future even when everything looked threatening. Here that did not seem right. Certainly the whole affair could be viewed as a joke, a crude practical joke arranged by his fellow bank employees for some unknown reason, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday. That was possible, naturally; perhaps he need only laugh in the guards' faces somehow and they would join in, perhaps they were porters from the street corner, whom they rather resembled—nevertheless, on this occasion, virtually from his first sight of the guard Franz, he had resolved to surrender not the slightest advantage he might possess over these people. That he might later be accused of failing to appreciate a joke struck K. as a very small danger. But he recalled—though learning from experience was otherwise no habit of his—a few incidents, insignificant in themselves, in which he had deliberately behaved incautiously, unlike his friends, without the faintest sense of the possible consequences, and the outcome had punished him for it. That must not recur, at least on this occasion; if this was a comedy, he would take his part.

For now his freedom remained. “Excuse me,” he said, hurrying between the guards into his own room. Behind him he heard: “He seems a sensible fellow.” Once inside, he tugged open the drawers of his desk. Everything lay in excellent order, yet in his agitation the very documents he wanted, his identification papers, eluded him at first. Eventually he located his cycling permit and was about to take it to the guards, but then it seemed too insignificant a document; he went on looking until his birth certificate turned up. As he returned to the other room, the door opposite was just opening to admit Mrs Grubach. She appeared only briefly: at the sight of K. she evidently grew embarrassed, apologised, vanished, and closed the door with extreme care. K. had barely managed to say: “Please, do come inside.” Now he stood amid the room with his documents, his eyes still on the door, which remained shut, until a call from the guards startled him out of it. They were sitting at the little table beside the open window and, he now realised, eating his breakfast. “What stopped her coming in?” he asked. “It isn't allowed,” the tall guard said. “You are under arrest, remember.” “How is my arrest possible? And in this fashion, of all things?” “So you're starting all over again,” said the guard, dipping buttered bread into the pot of honey. “Questions of that sort receive no answer from us.” K. replied: “Answer them you must.” “These are my identity documents; now let me see yours, and above all the warrant authorising my arrest.” “Heaven preserve us!” the guard said. “You simply cannot accept your position, can you? And you seem bent on provoking us to no purpose, when at present we are probably nearer to you than anybody else is.” “That is how things stand, do believe it,” Franz said; instead of raising the coffee cup in his hand to his lips, he gave K. a prolonged look, probably full of significance but quite incomprehensible. Without intending to, K. let himself engage in a silent exchange of looks with Franz, but then tapped his documents after all and said: “My identification is here.” “What concern is that of ours?” the tall guard now exclaimed. “A child would behave better. What are you after? Do you hope to hurry your great accursed case to its conclusion by debating identification and arrest warrants with us guards? We're employees of the lowest rank, scarcely able to make sense of an identity document; our sole connection with your affair is that we are paid to watch over you ten hours a day. Nothing more than that. Even so, we can understand that the high authorities we serve investigate both the grounds for an arrest and the person to be arrested most carefully before ordering it. Mistakes don't occur there. So far as I know our authority—and only its bottom ranks are known to me—it doesn't go looking for guilt among the population. Guilt attracts it, as the law puts it, and then it has to send us guards out. Such is the law. Where could a mistake enter into that?” “That law is unknown to me,” K. said. “So much the worse for your position,” the guard replied. “Perhaps it exists only in your minds,” K. said. He was trying somehow to find his way into the guards' thinking, to turn it to his advantage or establish himself within it. The guard dismissed his effort with, “Its effects will teach you.” Franz broke in: “Willem, listen to this: by his own admission he is ignorant of the law, yet he claims innocence all the same.” The other replied: “Exactly, but explaining anything to him is impossible.” K. ceased replying. Must I, he thought, let the chatter of these most subordinate functionaries—they admit that is what they are—confuse me further? Whatever else, they're talking about matters beyond their comprehension. Only stupidity allows them such certainty. A few words exchanged with somebody on my own level will clarify everything incomparably better than the longest conversations with these two. Several times he paced the unoccupied part of the room. Across the way he saw that the old woman had dragged to the window an even older man and was holding her arms round him. This public spectacle must be stopped, K. felt. “Bring me before your superior,” he demanded. “When he wants you, and no sooner,” replied the guard who had been called Willem. “For the present,” he added, “my advice is to return to your room, keep quiet, and wait for the decision about you. We advise you to collect yourself instead of scattering your thoughts on useless matters; much is going to be demanded of you. Our friendliness deserved better treatment than you have given us. You have forgotten that, whatever else we may be, for the moment at least we are free men and you are not, which is a considerable advantage. Nevertheless, provided you have the money, we are willing to fetch you a little breakfast from the café across the way.”

K. remained motionless for a short while, leaving the offer unanswered. If he opened the door into the next room, or even the door to the entrance hall, the two might not dare to intervene; perhaps forcing the issue would settle everything most simply. But perhaps they would seize him after all, and once he had been thrown down, the superiority he still enjoyed over them in certain respects would be lost as well. He therefore chose the certainty of a resolution that the natural course of events must bring, and returned to his room. Neither he nor the guards had spoken another word.

Throwing himself onto the bed, he picked up from the washstand a fine apple he had laid out for breakfast the previous evening. Now it constituted his entire breakfast, and was certainly far better, he assured himself with the first large bite, than anything the guards might have graciously obtained for him from that dirty all-night café. He felt comfortable and confident. True, he was absent from his duties at the bank this morning, but his relatively senior position there made that easy to excuse. Ought he give the real explanation? He intended to. If he was disbelieved, which would be understandable in this instance, Mrs Grubach could testify for him, as could the two old people across the way, who were probably now on the march to the window opposite this one. It surprised K.—from the guards' standpoint, at any rate—that they had driven him into his room and left him alone, with several ways of killing himself at his disposal. From his own standpoint, though, he simultaneously wondered what possible reason he could have for doing so. Because those two were sitting next door and had intercepted his breakfast, perhaps? Suicide would have been so pointless that its very pointlessness would have made him incapable of it, even had he wanted it. Were the guards' mental limitations less conspicuous, one might have supposed that this same conviction had reassured them that leaving him alone presented no danger. Let them watch now, if they chose, as he went over to the little wall cupboard where he kept a good spirit, drained one small glass to replace his breakfast and assigned a second the task of bolstering his courage—the latter merely as a precaution, against the unlikely eventuality of its being needed.

Just then a shout from the adjoining room startled him so violently that his teeth struck the glass. “The supervisor wants you,” came the call. Only the shouting had frightened him: that abrupt, clipped military shout, which he would never have thought the guard Franz capable of producing. The order itself was most welcome. “At last!” he shouted back, locked the cupboard, and hurried straight into the next room. The two guards stood there and, as though nothing could be more natural, chased him back into his own. “Whatever are you thinking of?” they cried. “Going before the supervisor in your shirt? He'll have you thrashed, and us along with you.” “Damn you, leave me alone!” K. exclaimed, already forced back as far as his wardrobe. “When people are attacked in bed, you can't expect to find them in their best clothes.” “That makes no difference,” said the guards. Whenever K. shouted they became perfectly calm, almost sorrowful, and this disconcerted him or in a way recalled him to his senses. “Ridiculous formalities!” he still muttered, but was already lifting a coat from a chair. He held it a moment in both hands, as though submitting it for the guards' approval. They shook their heads. “A black coat is required,” they said. K. flung the coat down and remarked—he did not himself know in what sense he meant it—“We haven't reached the main hearing yet.” Smiling, the guards nevertheless repeated their insistence: “A black coat is required.” “If that gets this business moving, I'm agreeable,” K. said. He opened the wardrobe himself, searched for some time among his numerous clothes, and chose his best black suit, a lounge suit whose cut at the waist had almost caused a sensation among his acquaintances; then he took out a different shirt as well and began dressing with care. Secretly he believed he had accelerated the whole business by the guards' forgetting to make him bathe. He watched them in case it should occur to them after all, but of course it never entered their heads. Willem, however, did remember to send Franz to the supervisor with word that K. was dressing.

Fully dressed, he had to walk just ahead of Willem, through the empty adjoining room and into the one beyond, where both halves of the door already stood open. As K. knew perfectly well, this room had recently been taken by a Miss Bürstner, a typist who generally left for work very early and returned home late, and with whom he had exchanged scarcely anything beyond greetings. Her bedside table had now been moved out into the room's centre to serve as a table for the proceedings, and behind it sat the supervisor, his legs crossed, one arm laid along the chair back.

Three young men occupied a corner of the room, examining Miss Bürstner's photographs, which were tucked into a mat hanging against the wall. A white blouse hung from the handle of the open window. At the window opposite, the two old people were once again leaning out, but their party had grown: behind them stood a man who towered over both, his shirt open at the chest, squeezing and twisting his reddish pointed beard between his fingers. “Josef K.?” the supervisor asked, possibly just to draw K.'s wandering gaze to himself. K. nodded. “This morning's occurrences have presumably astonished you considerably?” the supervisor asked, using both hands meanwhile to shift about the few objects on the bedside table—a candle and matches, a book, a pincushion—as though they were equipment necessary to his proceedings. “Certainly,” K. said, seized by the pleasant feeling of finally facing a reasonable man with whom he could discuss his affair, “certainly I am astonished, though by no means considerably.” “Not considerably?” the supervisor asked, now placing the candle centrally on the table and arranging the remaining objects around it. “Perhaps you misunderstand,” K. hastened to add. “What I mean—” He broke off here to look about for an armchair. “May I sit?” he asked. “That is not customary,” the supervisor replied. “What I mean,” K. now continued without another pause, “is that of course I am considerably astonished, but after thirty years in the world, making one's own way as I have had to, one grows hardened to surprises and doesn't take them too badly. Least of all today's.” “Why today's least of all?” “I'm not saying I regard the whole business as a joke; the arrangements seem much too extensive for that. Everybody in this boarding house would have to be involved, together with all of you, which would take it beyond the limits of a joke. So that isn't what I am saying.” “Quite correct,” said the supervisor, inspecting the matchbox to see how many matches it contained. “On the other hand,” K. continued, addressing everybody now and wishing he could even turn the three at the photographs towards himself, “on the other hand it cannot be a matter of much importance either. My reason for saying so is that I am accused, yet can discover no guilt whatsoever on which an accusation could be based. Even that, though, is a secondary matter. The central question is: who has accused me? Which authority is conducting these proceedings? Do you hold official positions? None of you is in uniform, unless yours”—here he turned to Franz—“can be called a uniform, but it looks more like a travelling suit. I demand clarity on these points, and I feel certain that once they are clarified we shall be able to take leave of one another with the utmost cordiality.” The supervisor slapped the matchbox down. “You are very seriously mistaken,” he said. “These gentlemen and I are entirely incidental to your affair; indeed we know next to nothing about it. Even if we wore the most regulation uniforms imaginable, your situation would be no worse. Nor can I tell you that you are accused; more precisely, I don't know whether you are. Your arrest is a fact, but my knowledge goes no further. The guards may have chattered about something else; in that event it was mere chatter. Although I am not answering your questions, I can offer advice: give less thought to us and to what is to happen to you, and more to yourself. And don't make such an uproar over your sense of innocence; it spoils the otherwise not unfavourable impression you give. Generally, too, greater restraint in speaking would be advisable. Almost everything you said just now could have been inferred from your conduct had you spoken only a few words, and in any case it was hardly greatly to your advantage.”

K. fixed his eyes on the supervisor. Was somebody possibly younger than himself giving him schoolroom instruction here? Was a reprimand his reward for frankness? And still no information about the cause of his arrest or who had ordered it?

Some agitation took hold of him. He paced about unhindered, pushed his cuffs back, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed the three gentlemen and said, “This really makes no sense,” at which they turned and looked at him with serious but accommodating expressions, and finally stopped once more before the supervisor's table. “Hasterer, the public prosecutor, is a close friend of mine,” he said. “May I telephone him?” “Certainly,” the supervisor said, “though I cannot see what purpose that would serve, unless you have some private business to discuss with him.” “What purpose?” K. cried, more dismayed than angry. “Who are you, exactly? You ask for a purpose while staging the most senseless performance imaginable. Wouldn't it soften a stone? First these gentlemen invade my room; now they sit or stand about and make me put on a display of accomplished horsemanship for you. What purpose would calling a public prosecutor serve when I am supposedly under arrest? Very well, I shall make no call.” “Oh, please do,” said the supervisor, extending a hand towards the entrance hall, where the telephone was. “By all means telephone.” “No, I've lost the wish to,” K. said, and went to the window. The group opposite still occupied their window; only now that K. had approached his did their peaceful spectatorship seem slightly disturbed. The old people tried to rise, but the man behind soothed them. “We have spectators over there as well,” K. called very loudly to the supervisor, pointing out with his forefinger. Then he shouted across: “Get away from there!” All three immediately retreated several paces; the two old people even went behind the man, who screened them with his broad body and, judging by the movements of his mouth, was saying something inaudible at that distance. They did not disappear altogether, however, but seemed to await a chance to approach the window again unnoticed. “Intrusive, inconsiderate people!” K. said, turning back into the room. A sidelong glance suggested that the supervisor might agree with him. Equally, he might not have listened at all: one hand was pressed flat against the table, and he seemed to be comparing the lengths of its fingers. Both guards were sitting on a trunk draped with an ornamental cover, rubbing their knees. The three young men stood with their hands planted on their hips and gazed aimlessly around. The silence was that of some forgotten office. “Well then, gentlemen,” K. called—for an instant it seemed that he bore them all on his shoulders—“judging by your appearance, my affair must be concluded. I consider it best to stop deliberating on whether your conduct was justified, and end the matter amicably by shaking hands all round. If you share that view, then please—” He stepped up to the supervisor's table and offered his hand. The supervisor raised his eyes, bit at his lips, and looked at the offered hand. K. still believed he would take it. Instead, he got up, picked up a stiff round hat lying on Miss Bürstner's bed, and carefully lowered it onto his head with both hands, in the manner of someone trying on a new hat. While doing this he remarked to K.: “Everything looks so simple in your eyes!” “An amicable conclusion to the matter, was that your proposal? No, no, that really cannot be arranged. Which certainly does not mean I am telling you to despair. No, why would you? Your arrest is all, nothing beyond that. My business was to inform you of it; I have done so and observed your response as well. That suffices for today, and we may take our leave, provisionally of course. You presumably want to go to the bank now?” “To the bank?” K. asked. “But I thought you had arrested me.” His questioning had a defiant note: although his offered hand had been rejected, these people seemed to have less and less hold over him, particularly now that the supervisor was on his feet. He was playing with them. Should they leave, he intended to pursue them as far as the building's front door and offer himself for arrest. That was why he repeated: “Since I am under arrest, how am I supposed to go to the bank?” “Oh, I see,” said the supervisor, already at the door. “You have misconstrued me. Arrested you certainly are, but this is not meant to prevent you from attending to your profession. Nor is your customary manner of living to be impeded.” “Then being arrested isn't such a terrible thing,” K. said, approaching him closely. “I never suggested otherwise,” the man replied. “In that case, even announcing the arrest hardly seems to have been necessary,” K. said, drawing closer still. The others had approached as well. They were all gathered now in a confined space by the door. “It was my duty,” the supervisor said. “A stupid duty,” K. retorted, refusing to yield. “Possibly,” the supervisor replied, “but let us avoid wasting time on such remarks. My assumption was that you wanted to go to the bank. Since you attend to every word, I shall add that I am not compelling you to go there; I merely assumed you wished to. To facilitate that, and make your arrival at the bank as inconspicuous as possible, I have kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, here at your disposal.” “What?” K. exclaimed, staring at the three. These colourless, anaemic young men, still associated in his mind only with the group beside the photographs, were indeed employees of his bank. Colleagues was too strong a term, already revealing a gap in the supervisor's omniscience, but junior bank employees they certainly were. How could he have failed to notice? How absorbed the supervisor and guards must have made him for him not to recognise these three: stiff Rabensteiner, swinging his hands; fair-haired Kullich with his sunken eyes; and Kaminer with that intolerable smile produced by a chronic muscular strain. After a moment K. said, “Good morning,” and shook hands with the gentlemen, who bowed correctly. “I failed to recognise you altogether. So now we shall go to work, shall we?” They nodded eagerly and with laughter, as though this was what they had been awaiting all along. Only when K. missed his hat, left in his room, did all of them run off one behind another to fetch it, suggesting a certain embarrassment after all. K. stood watching through the two open doorways. Last, naturally, came indifferent Rabensteiner, who had merely adopted an elegant trot. Kaminer handed over the hat, and K. had to remind himself expressly—as he often had to at the bank—that Kaminer did not smile on purpose; indeed, smiling deliberately was quite beyond him. In the entrance hall Mrs Grubach, looking by no means particularly guilty, opened the flat's door for the whole party. As so often before, K. glanced down at her apron string, which cut so needlessly deep into her ample body. Downstairs, watch in hand, he decided on a motorcar so as not to prolong unnecessarily a delay already amounting to half an hour. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch one. The other two were plainly trying to distract K. when Kullich suddenly pointed to the doorway of the building opposite. The tall man with the fair pointed beard was just appearing there; for an instant, a little embarrassed to be visible at his full height, he drew back and leaned against the wall. The old people were probably still on the stairs. K. resented Kullich's drawing attention to the man, whom he himself had already noticed, had even expected. “Don't look over there,” he snapped, unaware how remarkable such a manner of speaking was towards independent men. No explanation proved necessary, however, for the motorcar arrived just then; they got in and drove off. Now K. remembered that he had quite failed to notice the supervisor and guards leaving. The supervisor had hidden the three clerks from his attention, and then the clerks had hidden the supervisor. This showed little presence of mind, and he resolved to observe himself more closely in that respect. Even so, he involuntarily turned and leaned out over the car's rear bodywork in the hope of still catching sight of the supervisor and guards. Almost immediately he faced forward again and settled comfortably in his corner, without having so much as attempted to look for anyone. Appearances notwithstanding, at that very moment some encouragement would have helped him, but the gentlemen now seemed tired. Rabensteiner looked out on the right, Kullich on the left; only Kaminer and his grin remained available, and unfortunately humanity forbade making a joke of that.

That spring K. generally spent his evenings in the following fashion: after work, if time still allowed—he usually remained at the office until nine—he took a short walk, alone or with other employees, then went to a beer house, where he sat at the regulars' table, mostly among older gentlemen, ordinarily until eleven. Exceptions did occur: the bank manager, for instance, who greatly valued his capacity for work and his trustworthiness, sometimes invited him for a drive or to dinner at his villa. Once weekly, moreover, K. visited a girl called Elsa. She waited tables in a wine bar through the night and well into the morning, and in the daytime received her visitors only in bed.

This evening, however—the day had passed quickly in strenuous work and numerous birthday wishes, both respectful and affectionate—K. intended to go straight home. Throughout the day's work he had thought about it in every little pause. Without quite knowing what he meant, he felt as though the morning's events had caused great disorder throughout Mrs Grubach's flat, and as though he in particular was needed to put it right. With order restored, every trace of those events would be effaced and everything would resume its accustomed course. The three clerks, especially, offered no cause for concern. They had sunk back into the bank's large body of employees and showed no perceptible alteration. K. had summoned them to his office repeatedly, separately and together, solely to observe them; he had always been able to dismiss them satisfied.

It was half past nine in the evening when he reached the building where he lived. In its doorway he encountered a young fellow standing with legs spread, smoking a pipe. “Who might you be?” K. immediately asked, bringing his face close to the fellow's, since little was visible in the passage's half-darkness. “The caretaker's son, sir,” the youth replied, removing his pipe and moving aside. “The caretaker's son?” K. echoed; his stick struck the floor impatiently. “Is there anything you require, sir? Should I call Father?” “No, no,” K. replied. Something forgiving had entered his voice, as if the fellow had committed a wrong and K. was pardoning him. “That's all right,” he added, and went on, though before ascending the stairs he turned for another look.

Nothing prevented him from going straight to his room; wishing to speak with Mrs Grubach, however, he first knocked on hers. She was sitting with a stocking she was knitting at the table, on which a pile of old stockings also lay. K. absently apologised for the late visit; Mrs Grubach, however, was most cordial and would hear no apology. She was always available to him, she said; he knew perfectly well that of all her lodgers he was the best and dearest. K. surveyed the room. It had been restored entirely to its former condition; even the breakfast things that had stood on the little window table that morning were already cleared away. Women's hands accomplish a great deal in silence, he thought. He himself might have smashed the crockery on the spot, but could certainly never have carried it out. He looked at Mrs Grubach with a measure of gratitude. “Why keep working at this hour?” he asked. Both were now seated at the table, and from time to time K. buried a hand among the stockings. “There's much to be done,” she said. “By day my lodgers have the use of me; only the evenings remain for putting my own things in order.” “Today I must have given you some quite exceptional work as well.” “How so?” she asked, growing a little more animated, her knitting idle in her lap. “Those men who were here this morning, I mean.” “Oh, that,” she said, resuming her calm. “That caused me no particular work.” K. silently watched her take up the knitting again. She seems surprised that I mention it, he thought; she seems to consider it improper for me to mention it. That makes speaking of it all the more important. Only with an old woman is such a conversation possible for me. “It certainly must have caused work,” he said at last, “but it won't happen again.” “No, it cannot happen again,” she said emphatically, smiling at him almost sadly. “Do you really mean that?” K. asked. “Yes,” she said more softly, “but above all you mustn't let it weigh on you so much. What doesn't happen in this world! Since you are speaking so confidentially to me, Mr K., I may as well confess that I listened a little behind the door, and the two guards also told me a few things. Your happiness is at stake, after all, and I truly care about that, perhaps more than I have any right to, being only your landlady. Well, I did hear something of it, but I cannot say it was anything especially dreadful. No. You have been arrested, certainly, but not in the way a thief is arrested. An arrest like a thief's is a terrible thing, but this arrest—. It strikes me as something scholarly; forgive me if that is foolish, but it strikes me as something scholarly, something I don't understand, though understanding it isn't necessary either.”

“There is nothing foolish in what you've said, Mrs Grubach. I agree with you in part, at least, except that my judgment of the whole affair is more severe: I don't even regard it as something scholarly, simply as nothing at all. I was caught off guard, that was the trouble. Had I got up immediately on waking, without letting Anna's absence unsettle me, and come to you regardless of anybody who might have tried to intercept me; had I breakfasted, say, in the kitchen for a change, and asked you to fetch my clothes from my room; had I behaved sensibly, in short, nothing further would have happened and whatever was trying to develop would have been stifled. But one is so ill prepared. At the bank, for example, I am prepared; something like this could never possibly happen to me there. My own attendant is available, the general telephone and my office telephone stand before me on the desk, people are constantly coming in, clients and employees alike, and besides—and above all—I am continuously engaged in the work there, which keeps my wits about me. Confronting such a business there would positively give me pleasure. Well, it has passed, and I really had no intention of discussing it further. I wanted only your judgment, a sensible woman's judgment, and I am very glad we agree. Now, though, you must give me your hand; agreement like this calls for a handshake to confirm it.”

Will she give me her hand, he wondered; the supervisor refused to give me his. He studied the woman with a different, more searching look than before. She rose because he had risen too, a little embarrassed because some of what K. had said was beyond her understanding. This embarrassment, however, made her say something quite unintended and quite out of place. “Do try not to let it weigh on you so, Mr K.,” she said, tears audible in her voice; naturally she forgot about the handshake as well. “I wasn't aware that I was letting it weigh on me,” K. replied, suddenly weary and recognising how worthless all this woman's agreement was.

At the doorway he asked one more question: “Has Miss Bürstner come home?” “No,” said Mrs Grubach. Along with this bare piece of information she offered a smile of belated, sensible sympathy. “She's at the theatre. Was there something you wanted of her? Could I give her a message?” “Oh, only a few words I wanted to exchange.” “Unfortunately I don't know when to expect her. Theatre evenings usually mean a late return.” “It doesn't matter at all,” K. said, already turning his lowered head towards the door to leave. “I merely wanted to apologise for making use of her room today.” “Quite unnecessary, Mr K.; you are too considerate. The young lady knows nothing about it. She left early this morning and has not returned since; meanwhile all has been tidied away. Look for yourself.” She opened Miss Bürstner's door. “Thank you, I believe you,” K. said, yet went over to the open doorway all the same. Moonlight shone quietly into the dark room. As far as one could tell, everything was indeed in its proper place; the blouse no longer hung from the window handle either. The pillows on the bed seemed remarkably high, partly lying in the moonlight. “The young lady often comes back late,” K. observed, looking at Mrs Grubach as if she were responsible. “Young people will be young people!” she said apologetically. “Of course, of course,” K. said, “but there can be too much of it.” “There can indeed,” Mrs Grubach said. “How right you are, Mr K. Possibly even in this instance. I certainly have no wish to slander Miss Bürstner. She is a good, dear girl, friendly, tidy, punctual, hardworking; I value all that greatly. One point remains true, though: greater pride and restraint would become her. Twice already this month I have seen her in out-of-the-way streets, each time with a different gentleman. It pains me to say so; before Almighty God, Mr K., you alone are hearing this from me, but I shan't be able to avoid speaking to the young lady herself about it as well. Nor is it the only thing that arouses my suspicions.” “You are completely mistaken,” K. said, scarcely able to hide his fury. “Besides, you have plainly misunderstood what I said about her. That was not my meaning. In fact I earnestly warn you against saying anything to her: you are utterly wrong. I know the young lady very well, and nothing of what you've said is true. But perhaps I am overstepping myself; I won't stop you. Tell her whatever you wish. Good night.” Pleadingly, Mrs Grubach called, “Mr K.,” and hurried after him as far as his already open door. “Speaking to her is not my intention yet. Naturally I mean to keep watching her first. I have only told you, in confidence, what I knew. After all, surely every lodger benefits from efforts to keep a boarding house respectable, and that is my sole intention.” “Respectable!” K. called through the gap in his door. “If a respectable boarding house is what you want, you must start by giving me notice.” He slammed the door then and paid no attention to a soft knock.

Instead, since he had no desire to sleep, he resolved to stay awake and use the opportunity to establish when Miss Bürstner returned. Perhaps, inappropriate though it might be, he could still exchange a few words with her then. At the window, leaning out and rubbing his weary eyes, it even occurred to him for an instant to punish Mrs Grubach: he could persuade Miss Bürstner that they should both give notice. Immediately, though, this struck him as an appalling overreaction, and he even suspected himself of seeking to change lodgings because of that morning's events. Nothing could have been more absurd or, above all, more futile and contemptible.

Tiring of the view of the deserted street, he stretched out on the sofa, first leaving his door slightly ajar so that from the sofa he could immediately see anyone entering the flat. Until about eleven he lay quietly there smoking a cigar. After that he could endure it no longer and went out into the entrance hall for a while, as though this might hasten Miss Bürstner's return. No special longing drew him to her; even her precise appearance escaped his memory. Nevertheless, speaking with her was now his wish, and her late return annoyed him by bringing disturbance and confusion even to the ending of this day. It was her fault, too, that he had had no evening meal and had missed his intended visit to Elsa. Both omissions could still be remedied, admittedly, by going now to the wine bar that employed her. He intended to do that later, after speaking with Miss Bürstner.

Half past eleven had already passed when footsteps became audible on the stairs. Absorbed in his thoughts, K. had been striding audibly about the entrance hall, treating it like his own quarters; he now took refuge behind his door. The arrival was Miss Bürstner. As she locked up, she drew a silk scarf more tightly about her narrow shoulders, shivering. In another moment she would be in her room, where he certainly had no right to intrude at midnight; he must address her now. Unfortunately he had neglected to switch on the electric light in his own room, so emerging from its darkness would look like an attack and at the very least give her a bad fright. Helpless, with no time to lose, he whispered through the crack: “Miss Bürstner.” It sounded like a plea rather than a summons. “Is somebody there?” she asked, looking about with wide eyes. “It's me,” K. said, stepping out. “Oh, Mr K.!” she said with a smile. “Good evening.” She offered her hand. “I wanted a few words with you; would you allow me them now?” “Now?” Miss Bürstner asked. “Is now necessary? Rather peculiar, surely?” “My wait for you began at nine.” “Well, the theatre kept me away. I knew nothing about you.” “The occasion for what I want to say only arose today.” “I see. Well, I have no objection in principle, except that I am almost dropping with tiredness. You may join me in my room briefly, then. A conversation out here is quite impossible: everybody would be woken, and I would find that more unpleasant for our sake than for theirs. Stay here while I put the light on in my room, then turn this one off.” K. complied, but still waited until she quietly invited him in once again from her room. “Take a seat,” she said, indicating the ottoman. She herself stayed upright by the bedpost despite her professed exhaustion, not even removing her small hat with its extravagant load of flowers. “Well, what was it you wanted? I'm really curious.” She crossed her legs lightly. “Perhaps you will say,” K. began, “that this wasn't urgent enough to discuss now, but—” “I never listen to preambles,” Miss Bürstner said. “That simplifies my task,” K. replied. “This morning your room was put into some disorder, in a sense through my fault. Strangers did it against my wishes, yet, as I say, the fault was mine; I wanted to ask your pardon for that.” “My room?” she asked, scrutinising K. instead of the room. “Yes,” he said. For the first time they now looked directly into each other's eyes. “How it happened is in itself hardly worth mentioning.” “But that's the interesting part,” Miss Bürstner replied. “No,” K. said. “Well,” she said, “I have no wish to pry into secrets. If you insist it isn't interesting, I won't dispute it. I gladly grant the pardon you request, especially since I can find no sign of disorder.” With her palms placed low against her hips she walked around the room, stopping at the mat that held the photographs. “Look here!” she exclaimed. “My photographs really have been muddled up. How unpleasant. So my room has been entered by somebody with no right to be here.” K. nodded, inwardly cursing the clerk Kaminer, who could never restrain his dreary, purposeless exuberance. “It's strange,” Miss Bürstner said, “that I should have to forbid you something you ought to forbid yourself: entering my room when I'm absent.” “But I explained, miss,” K. said, joining her beside the photographs, “that I wasn't the person who interfered with your photographs. Since you don't believe me, though, I must admit that the commission of inquiry brought three bank clerks with it, one of whom probably handled the photographs. I shall have him put out of the bank at the first opportunity.” She looked at him questioningly, so he added: “Yes, there was a commission of inquiry here.” “On your account?” she asked. “Yes,” K. answered. “Surely not!” she exclaimed, laughing. “Indeed there was,” K. said. “Do you take me for innocent, then?” “Well, innocent,” she said, “I wouldn't want to pronounce a judgment straight away that might have serious consequences. Besides, I hardly know you. All the same, somebody must be quite a criminal for a commission of inquiry to be sent after him at once. Yet you are at liberty—I infer from your composure, at least, that you haven't escaped from prison—so you cannot have committed a crime of that kind.” “Yes,” K. said, “but the commission might have concluded that I was innocent, or at any rate less guilty than they had supposed.” “Certainly, that is possible,” Miss Bürstner said, listening intently. “You see,” K. said, “your experience of legal affairs is limited.” “It is,” she replied, “and I've often regretted that, since I want to know everything, and legal affairs interest me enormously. The court has a peculiar attraction, doesn't it? But I shall certainly fill out my knowledge in that direction: next month I begin as a clerk in a lawyer's office.” “Excellent,” K. said. “Then you'll be able to give me a little help with my case.” “Possibly,” Miss Bürstner said. “Why shouldn't I? I enjoy putting my knowledge to use.” “I am serious about it, too,” K. said, “or at least as half-serious as you are. The affair is too petty to involve a lawyer, but an adviser would be very useful.” “Yes, but to advise you I would need to know what the affair is about,” she said. “That's the difficulty,” K. replied. “I don't know myself.” “Then you've been making fun of me,” she said, disproportionately disappointed. “Choosing this hour, so far into the night, was utterly unnecessary.” She left the photographs, beside which they had been together for so long. “But, miss,” K. said, “I'm not joking. Why won't you believe me? My entire knowledge is already yours; indeed I have gone beyond my knowledge, since no commission of inquiry was actually involved. I call it that for want of another name. No inquiry took place; a commission merely placed me under arrest.” Seated now on the ottoman, Miss Bürstner again began laughing. “How did it happen?” she wanted to know. “Dreadful,” K. said. But he was no longer thinking of that at all; he was wholly absorbed by the sight of her supporting her face with one hand, its elbow resting on the ottoman's cushion, while the other slowly stroked her hip. “That's too vague,” she said. “What's too vague?” K. asked. Then he remembered. “Would you like me to show you how it happened?” He wanted movement without having to leave. “I'm tired already,” she said. “You returned so late,” K. replied. “So it ends with my being reproached. Quite deservedly, too: I shouldn't have admitted you at this hour. As it turns out, there was no need.” “There was a need, as you are about to see,” K. said. “May I move your bedside table over here?” “Whatever are you thinking?” she asked. “Of course you may not!” “Then I cannot demonstrate it,” K. replied in agitation, as if an immeasurable injury were being done him. “Well, if your demonstration requires it, go ahead and move the little table,” she said, adding after a moment in a weaker voice: “I'm so tired that I allow more than is good.” K. placed the table centrally in the room and took a seat behind it. “You must picture everyone's position correctly; it's very interesting. I am the supervisor. Two guards are sitting on that trunk, and three young men are standing by the photographs. A white blouse hangs from the window handle—I mention that merely in passing. Now it begins. Ah, I am forgetting myself: the most important person, namely me, stands here before the table. The supervisor lounges in extreme comfort, legs crossed, his arm dangling over the chair back here, an unparalleled lout. And now it really does begin. He calls in a manner meant to rouse a sleeper, fairly yelling; regrettably I shall have to yell too, so that you can appreciate it. It's only my name he shouts, incidentally.” Listening with laughter, Miss Bürstner raised her forefinger to her lips to prevent him shouting, but she was too late. K. had entered too deeply into his role. Slowly he called, “Josef K.”—not as loudly as he had threatened, admittedly, but still in such a way that the cry, suddenly released, seemed only gradually to spread through the room.

Several knocks then sounded at the adjoining room's door, forceful, brief and evenly spaced. Miss Bürstner went pale and pressed a hand against her heart. K.'s fright was especially severe because for a little while he remained quite incapable of thinking about anything except the morning's events and the girl to whom he was acting them out. Barely recovered, he bounded to her side and clasped her hand, whispering: “There is nothing to fear; I shall set it all right. Who can possibly be there, though? The adjoining room is merely the sitting room, with nobody sleeping in it.” “Someone does,” she whispered into his ear. “A nephew of Mrs Grubach's has slept there since yesterday, an army captain. There happens to be no other vacant room. I'd forgotten it myself. That shouting of yours—was it necessary! It has made me miserable.” “You need not be miserable,” K. answered; as she dropped back against the cushion, he planted a kiss on her brow. “Away with you, away!” she said, quickly raising herself once more. “Please leave, do leave. What do you want? He is listening at the door, he hears everything. How you torment me!” “I won't leave,” K. said, “until you have calmed down a little. Come to the other corner; he won't hear us there.” She allowed him to lead her over. “You fail to consider,” he said, “that this may be an inconvenience for you, but it presents no danger whatsoever. You know how Mrs Grubach positively worships me and believes whatever I say without question; she is the one who decides in this affair, especially since the captain is her nephew. She depends on me in other respects, too: she has borrowed a substantial sum from me. Whatever explanation for our being together you propose, I will accept it, provided it serves the purpose at all, and I guarantee to make Mrs Grubach believe it—not merely profess belief in public, but believe it sincerely and truly. You need not spare me in the slightest. If you want it said that I assaulted you, that is what Mrs Grubach will be told, and she will believe it without losing her trust in me; that is how attached she is.” Miss Bürstner stood silent, a little slumped, looking at the floor before her. “Why shouldn't she believe that I assaulted you?” K. added. Before him he saw her reddish hair, parted, puffed low and held firmly together. He expected her eyes to turn towards him. Instead, maintaining her position, she spoke: “Pardon me. What frightened me was the sudden knocking, not so much the consequences the captain's presence might have. After your shout it was so quiet, and then the knocks came; that's why I was so startled. I was sitting near the door, too, so it was almost beside me. Your proposals have my thanks, but not my acceptance. I can answer for whatever happens in my room, to anybody at all. It surprises me that you don't notice how insulting your suggestions are to me, alongside the good intentions which of course I recognise. Now please leave and let me be alone; I need that even more than before. The few minutes you requested have become half an hour and more.” K. took her hand, then held her wrist. “But you aren't angry with me?” he asked. She brushed his hand away. “No, no; I am never angry with anyone.” He reached for her wrist again; this time she allowed it and led him like that towards the door. He was firmly resolved to leave. Yet on reaching the door he faltered, as though he had not expected a door there. Miss Bürstner used the moment to free herself, open it, slip into the entrance hall and say quietly from there: “Please come now. Look”—she indicated the captain's door, beneath which light was showing—“he's put his light on and is amusing himself at our expense.” “I'm coming,” K. said. He hurried forward, seized her, and kissed her lips, then all over her face, like a thirsty animal sweeping its tongue over spring water it has at last discovered. Finally he kissed the front of her neck, at the throat, and kept his lips there for a long time. A sound from the captain's room made him glance up. “I'll leave now,” he said. He wanted to address her by her given name, but did not know it. She nodded wearily and, already half turned away, left him her hand to kiss as though unaware of it, then went bent forward into her room. Soon afterwards K. was in bed. Sleep came quickly; before it did he reflected a little on his conduct, with which he was satisfied, although he wondered why he was not more satisfied still. On Miss Bürstner's account the captain caused him serious concern.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: K. had been informed by telephone that a brief examination of his case would take place the following Sunday. He was told that these examinations would now follow regularly, if perhaps not every week, then at frequent intervals. On the one hand, it was in the general interest to bring the case to a swift conclusion; on the other, the examinations had to be thorough in every respect, yet, because of the strain involved, must never last too long. That was why they had chosen the solution of brief examinations following one another in quick succession. Sunday had been designated as the day for examination so as not to interfere with K.'s professional work. They assumed he agreed; if he preferred another appointment, they would accommodate him as far as possible. The examinations could, for instance, also take place at night, though K. would probably not be fresh enough then. In any event, they would keep to Sunday unless K. objected. It went without saying that he absolutely must attend; surely there was no need to point that out to him. He was given the number of the house where he was to appear. It was in a remote suburban street where K. had never been.

On receiving this communication K. replaced the receiver without a reply. He resolved at once to attend on Sunday; it was certainly necessary, for the case was getting under way and he must oppose it. This initial examination was also to be the final one. He was still standing thoughtfully beside the telephone when he heard the deputy manager's voice behind him. The man wanted to make a call, and K. was blocking his access. “Bad news?” the deputy manager asked casually, less to learn anything than to dislodge K. from the instrument. “No, no,” K. replied, stepping aside but remaining there. The deputy manager lifted the receiver and, while waiting to be connected, spoke across it: “A question, Mr K.: would you give me the pleasure of joining a sailing party on my boat on Sunday morning? There will be quite a gathering, certainly some people you know. Hesterer, the public prosecutor, among others. Will you join us? Do come!” K. tried to attend to the words. They mattered to him: an invitation from the deputy manager, with whom he had never got along particularly well, was an attempt at reconciliation and showed how important K. had become at the bank, how highly its second-ranking official valued his friendship, or at least his neutrality. Offering this invitation humbled the deputy manager, even if he had offered it merely across the telephone receiver while awaiting his connection. Yet K. had to follow it with a second humiliation. “Many thanks!” he said. “Unfortunately Sunday is already taken; I have another obligation.” “A pity,” the deputy manager said, turning to his call, which had just been connected. The conversation was a long one, but in his distraction K. remained beside the telephone throughout. Only when the deputy manager rang off did he start, and, to give some slight justification for standing there uselessly, he said: “Someone just telephoned asking me to come somewhere, but forgot to specify an hour.” “Why not ask them again?” the deputy manager suggested. “It is of no great importance,” K. said, further undermining his already inadequate excuse. As the deputy manager walked away he spoke about other matters. K. forced himself to respond, but chiefly considered that nine on Sunday morning would be the best time to arrive, since all courts began work then on weekdays.

Sunday brought dull weather. K. was exhausted: a celebration among the regulars had kept him at the inn far into the night, and he had very nearly overslept. Hastily, without leisure to reflect or put together the various plans devised during the week, he dressed and ran without breakfast to the suburb he had been directed to. Curiously, despite having little time to look about, he encountered all three employees involved in his affair, Rabensteiner, Kullich and Kaminer. A tram carried the first two across his path; Kaminer was seated on a café terrace and, precisely as K. passed, leaned inquisitively over its railing. They probably all watched him go, wondering at their superior's running. Some sort of defiance had prevented K. from taking a vehicle. In this affair of his he abhorred every kind of outside assistance, however slight; nor did he want to call on anybody and thus confide in them even in the remotest degree. Finally, he had not the least desire to abase himself before the commission of inquiry by excessive punctuality. Yet here he was running to arrive as nearly as possible at nine, although he had not even been summoned for a particular hour.

He had imagined that some sign—of which he himself had formed no clear notion—or some distinctive bustle at the entrance would allow him to recognise the building from far away. But Juliusstraße, where it was supposed to be, and at whose beginning he paused a moment, had almost uniformly similar buildings on either side: tall, grey tenements housing poor people. On this Sunday morning most windows were occupied. Men in shirtsleeves leaned out smoking, or held little children carefully and tenderly at the ledge. Other windows were piled high with bedding, above which a woman's dishevelled head would briefly appear. People called across the street to one another; one such call provoked loud laughter immediately above K. At regular intervals along the long street stood small shops selling assorted foodstuffs, situated below street level and reached by a few steps. Women passed through the shop doors in both directions, while others chatted on the steps. A fruit seller, praising his wares to the windows above, was as inattentive as K. and almost knocked him down with his barrow. Just then a gramophone, discarded by some better neighbourhood, began to play with murderous noise.

K. went farther into the street, slowly, as though he now had time, or as though the examining magistrate could see him from some window and therefore knew he had arrived. It was shortly after nine. The house was quite a way along; it was almost unusually extensive, and the entrance for vehicles in particular was high and wide. It was evidently intended for the goods wagons serving the various warehouses, now locked, which surrounded the large courtyard and bore the names of firms, some of which K. knew through the bank's business. Taking a closer interest in all these external details than was his habit, he also stopped for a little while at the entrance to the courtyard. Nearby, a barefoot man sat on a crate reading a newspaper. Two boys were rocking on a handcart. A frail young girl in a night jacket stood at a pump, looking at K. as the water flowed into her jug. In one corner of the courtyard a line was being stretched between two windows, with the washing to be dried already hanging on it. A man stood below, directing the work with a few shouted instructions.

K. turned towards the stairs to reach the examination room, but stopped again, for besides this staircase he could see three other stair entrances in the courtyard, and a small passage at the far end seemed to lead to a second courtyard as well. He was annoyed that they had not told him more precisely where the room was. It was a strange negligence or indifference with which they treated him, and he intended to state that very loudly and clearly. In the end he went up the first staircase after all, playing in his mind with the remembered remark of the guard Willem that the court was attracted by guilt, from which it really followed that the examination room must be on whichever staircase K. happened to choose.

During his ascent he disturbed numerous children playing on the stairs; they glared at him as he walked through their ranks. “If ever I come back here,” he told himself, “I must bring either sweets to win their favour or my stick to beat them.” Just below the first floor he even had to wait a while for a ball to finish rolling. Meanwhile two small boys, with the crafty faces of grown ruffians, clung to his trouser legs; shaking them loose would have meant hurting them, and he feared their screaming.

The actual search started on the first floor. Since he could hardly ask for the commission of inquiry, he invented a carpenter called Lanz—the name occurred to him because it belonged to Mrs Grubach's nephew, the captain—and planned to ask at every flat whether a carpenter of that name lived there, thus giving himself an opportunity to look inside the rooms. Usually this proved possible without any pretext: almost every door stood open, with children running through them in both directions. Most rooms were small, with a single window, and served as kitchens too. Some women held babies on one arm while tending the stove with their free hand. Half-grown girls, seemingly wearing nothing but aprons, were the busiest in running back and forth. Beds remained occupied in every room, by the sick, by sleepers, or by people stretched out in their clothes. Where doors were shut K. knocked and asked whether this was the home of a carpenter called Lanz. Usually a woman opened, heard him out, and turned towards someone rising from a bed inside: “The gentleman wants to know whether a carpenter called Lanz lives here.” “A carpenter called Lanz?” the person in bed would ask. “Yes,” K. would reply, although clearly no commission of inquiry was here, so his task at that door was finished. Many assumed he was deeply anxious to find the carpenter and reflected for a long time. They offered a carpenter with another surname, or a name bearing the faintest resemblance to Lanz; they inquired of neighbours or accompanied K. to a distant door, behind which such a man might, they thought, be subletting a room, or where somebody might provide better information than they could. Eventually K. scarcely needed to ask for himself any more, but was drawn in this fashion from floor to floor. He regretted the scheme that had at first seemed so practical. Below the fifth floor he resolved to abandon his search, said goodbye to a friendly young workman who wished to lead him further up, and started down. Then the futility of the entire undertaking annoyed him afresh; he turned back once more and knocked at the fifth floor's first door. In the little room the first thing to meet his eyes was a large wall clock already indicating ten. “Does a carpenter named Lanz live here?” he asked. “This way, please,” said a young woman with shining black eyes, who was washing children's linen in a bucket; with her wet hand she indicated the open doorway into the next room.

K. thought he was entering a meeting. People of the most varied kinds crowded a moderately sized room with two windows; nobody paid the newcomer any attention. Just below the ceiling a gallery ran round it, equally crammed, where people could stand only bent over, their heads and backs pressing against the ceiling. Finding the air too close, K. withdrew and told the young woman, who had probably misunderstood: “My inquiry was about a carpenter, a certain Lanz?” “Yes,” the woman replied. “Please step inside.” He might have disregarded her invitation, except that she came towards him and grasped the handle. “I have to close up after you,” she said. “Further admissions are forbidden.” “Very sensible,” K. observed. “Though it's overcrowded already.” Nevertheless he went back in.

A hand reached for K. from between two men talking just inside the door—one was making the motion of counting out money with both hands extended far in front of him, while the other stared sharply into his eyes. It belonged to a small, rosy-cheeked boy. “Come, come,” he said. K. let the boy lead him. It turned out that a narrow passage remained clear through the milling crowd, perhaps dividing two parties; this was also suggested by the fact that in the front rows to right and left K. saw scarcely a face turned towards him, but only the backs of people directing their words and gestures solely to others of their own party. Most were dressed in black, in old Sunday coats hanging long and loose. Only these clothes puzzled K.; otherwise he would have taken the whole thing for a local political meeting.

At the far end of the hall, to which K. was being led, a small table stood crossways on a very low platform, likewise crowded. Behind it, near the platform's edge, sat a short, fat, wheezing man, conversing amid great laughter with somebody standing behind him; this other man leaned an elbow on the chair back, his legs crossed. Occasionally the seated man flung an arm up, as if caricaturing somebody. The boy guiding K. found it difficult to deliver his message. Twice he had risen on tiptoe to try, without attracting the attention of the man above. Only when somebody else on the platform pointed the boy out did the man turn, bend down and listen to his quiet report. He then produced his watch and glanced quickly towards K. He said: “You are late by sixty-five minutes.” K. intended a reply but found no opportunity: the man had barely stopped talking when the right half of the hall erupted in a general grumble. Raising his voice, the man repeated, “You are late by sixty-five minutes,” and glanced briefly down into the hall as well. The grumbling immediately intensified; since he said nothing further, it subsided only gradually. The hall was now much quieter than when K. entered. Only the gallery continued its comments unabated. As far as anything could be distinguished up there through the dimness, haze and dust, those people seemed more poorly dressed than the people below. Some had brought cushions to place between their heads and the ceiling, protecting themselves from painful pressure.

K. had resolved to spend more time observing than speaking, so he forwent any defence against the supposed lateness and said merely: “Late I may be; here I am now.” Applause followed, again from the hall's right half. “Easily won over,” K. thought. Only the silence on the left, directly behind him, disturbed him; from there came no more than isolated claps. He considered what he might say to gain everybody at once, or, if that proved impossible, at least to gain the others occasionally as well.

“Yes,” said the man, “but I am no longer obliged to question you at this point”—again the grumbling, though this time misleadingly, for he waved the people quiet and continued—“nevertheless, as an exception, I shall still do so today. Lateness of this kind must not recur. Now step up here!” Somebody leapt down from the platform, making a place for K. to climb onto. He stood pressed close against the table. So great was the crowd's pressure behind him that he had to resist it to avoid pushing the examining magistrate's table, and possibly the magistrate himself, off the platform.

The examining magistrate paid no heed to this, but sat quite comfortably in his chair. After a final word to the man behind him, he reached for a little notebook, the only object his table held. It resembled a school exercise book, old and misshapen through constant turning of its pages. “Well then,” he said, leafing through it and addressing K. in the manner of a statement of fact, “you are a house painter?” “No,” K. replied. “Chief authorised signatory at a large bank.” This answer provoked such hearty laughter from the right-hand party that K. had to join in. People braced their hands against their knees and shook as though suffering violent coughing fits. Even a few in the gallery laughed. Thoroughly enraged, the examining magistrate apparently lacked power over those below and tried to compensate at the gallery's expense. He sprang up and made threatening gestures towards it; above his eyes his normally inconspicuous eyebrows now crowded thick, black and large.

But the left half of the hall was still quiet. The people stood there in rows, their faces turned towards the platform, listening to the words exchanged above as calmly as to the noise of the other party; they even tolerated individuals from their own ranks occasionally joining in with the other side. The people of the left-hand party, who were fewer in number, might at bottom be just as insignificant as those on the right, but the calmness of their behaviour made them seem more important. When K. now began speaking, he was convinced that he was speaking in their spirit.

“Examining magistrate, you asked if house painting was my occupation—or, to be precise, you made no inquiry but declared outright that it was. That typifies the entire manner of the proceedings brought against me. You may object that they aren't proceedings at all. Quite rightly: they become proceedings only through my recognising them as such. For this moment, then, I do recognise them, in a sense out of pity. Pity is the only possible response if one is to give them any attention whatever. I am not calling these slipshod proceedings; I would merely offer you that description as an aid to self-knowledge.”

K. paused to look down into the hall. His words had been sharp, sharper than intended, but correct nevertheless. They deserved applause here or there; instead there was universal silence, an apparently tense anticipation of what would follow, perhaps a silence preparing an eruption that would end everything. It was distracting when the door at the hall's far end now opened and the young washerwoman entered, probably finished with her work. Despite all her care, she drew some eyes towards herself. Only the examining magistrate gave K. immediate pleasure, seeming directly struck by his words. Until now he had listened standing, having been surprised by K.'s address while on his feet to deal with the gallery. During the pause he lowered himself gradually into his chair, as though hoping to escape notice. He took up the notebook again, probably to steady his expression.

“That won't help,” K. went on. “Your little notebook, too, Mr Examining Magistrate, confirms what I'm saying.” Satisfied to hear only his own calm words in this unfamiliar gathering, K. even dared to take the notebook from the examining magistrate without further ado and lift it by a middle page with his fingertips, as though shrinking from it, so that the closely written, stained, yellow-edged pages hung down on either side. “These are the examining magistrate's records,” he said, letting the notebook drop onto the table. “By all means go on reading it, Mr Examining Magistrate. I'm truly not afraid of this ledger of guilt, although it's inaccessible to me, since I can only touch it with two fingertips and cannot take it in my hand.” It could only be a sign of deep humiliation—or at least it had to be interpreted that way—that the examining magistrate reached for the notebook as it lay on the table, tried to put it somewhat in order, and took it up again to read.

The faces of the people in the front row were turned towards K. with such intentness that he looked down at them for a little while. They were all older men, some with white beards. Perhaps they were the ones who mattered, who could influence the whole gathering, which even the humiliation of the examining magistrate had not roused from the immobility into which it had sunk since K.'s speech began.

“What happened to me,” K. continued, a little more quietly than before, repeatedly searching the faces in the front row, which gave his speech a somewhat distracted air, “what happened to me is only an individual case, and as such not very important, since I don't take it too seriously. But it is a sign of proceedings such as are brought against many people. It is for them that I stand here, not for myself.”

He had raised his voice involuntarily. Somewhere someone clapped with upraised hands and shouted: “Bravo! Why not? Bravo! And bravo again!” Here and there the men in the front row reached into their beards; none turned round at the shout. K. attached no importance to it either, but was encouraged nevertheless. He no longer felt it necessary for everyone to applaud; it was enough if the gathering as a whole began thinking about the matter and only occasionally an individual was won over by persuasion.

“Success as a speaker is not my aim,” K. said, prompted by this reflection. “It would probably be beyond my reach anyway. The examining magistrate is doubtless far better at speaking; it belongs to his profession. I seek merely a public discussion of a public abuse. Listen: roughly ten days ago I was arrested. The fact of arrest itself makes me laugh, but that has no bearing here. Early in the morning I was attacked in bed; perhaps—and the magistrate's remark makes this quite possible—the order was to arrest some house painter, just as innocent as I, but they selected me. Two coarse guards occupied the room beside mine. Had I been a dangerous robber, no greater precautions could have been taken. These guards, moreover, were depraved rabble: they talked my ears off, solicited bribes, sought to coax my linen and clothing from me under false pretences, and wanted money supposedly to fetch me breakfast after shamelessly consuming my own before my eyes. Nor did it end there. I was brought before the supervisor in a third room, belonging to a lady I hold in high regard; I was obliged to witness that room being, so to speak, defiled by the presence of the guards and supervisor, on my account but through no fault of mine. Remaining calm was difficult. I managed it, however, and asked the supervisor in perfect calm—were he present, he would have to confirm this—the reason for my arrest. And how did that supervisor answer, whom I still see sitting in the lady's chair as the embodiment of the dullest arrogance? Gentlemen, essentially he gave no answer. Perhaps he really knew nothing; he had arrested me, and that satisfied him. He even went further, introducing into that lady's room three low-ranking employees of my bank, who occupied themselves with handling and disarranging photographs that belonged to her. Naturally their presence had another purpose as well: along with my landlady and her maid, they were to spread word of my arrest, injure my reputation among the public and, above all, undermine my position at the bank. None of this succeeded in the slightest. Even my landlady, a very simple person—I shall name her here with respect: she is Mrs Grubach—even Mrs Grubach had sufficient understanding to see that such an arrest means no more than an escapade committed in the street by inadequately supervised boys. I repeat: the entire affair caused me nothing beyond inconvenience and passing irritation. But might its consequences not have been worse?”

When K. paused here and looked towards the silent examining magistrate, he thought he noticed him just then signalling to someone in the crowd with a glance. K. smiled and said: “Here beside me, the examining magistrate is just giving one of you a secret signal. So there are people among you being directed from up here. I don't know whether that signal was supposed to produce hissing or applause, and by exposing the matter prematurely I am quite deliberately giving up the opportunity to learn what the signal means. It is a matter of complete indifference to me, and I publicly authorise the examining magistrate to command his paid employees down there in words spoken aloud, instead of with secret signals, saying, for example, one time: Now hiss, and the next: Now clap.”

The examining magistrate shifted back and forth in his chair, embarrassed or impatient. The man behind him, with whom he had been talking earlier, leaned towards him again, whether to encourage him in general or offer some particular advice. Below, people were talking quietly but animatedly. The two parties, which had earlier seemed to hold such opposite opinions, were mixing; some people pointed at K., others at the examining magistrate. The misty haze in the room was extremely trying; it even prevented a closer view of those standing farther away. It must have been particularly troublesome to the people in the gallery, who were forced, with timid sideways glances at the examining magistrate, to put quiet questions to the members of the gathering in order to learn more. The answers were given just as quietly, behind shielding hands.

“I'm nearly finished,” said K., banging his fist on the table because there was no bell. Startled by this, the heads of the examining magistrate and his adviser instantly flew apart. “I stand apart from this whole affair, so I can judge it calmly, and you may gain a great deal by listening to me, provided this supposed court matters to you at all. I ask you to postpone your discussions among yourselves of what I'm putting forward, because I have no time and shall soon leave.”

There was silence at once; K. already had that much command of the gathering. People were no longer shouting over one another as at the beginning; they were not even applauding any more, but they seemed convinced, or very nearly so.

“There is no doubt,” K. said very quietly, pleased by the strained attention of the entire gathering; in this silence there arose a rushing sound more stirring than the most ecstatic applause, “there is no doubt that behind every manifestation of this court—in my case, then, behind the arrest and today's examination—stands a large organisation. An organisation that employs not only corruptible guards, foolish supervisors and examining magistrates who are mediocre at best, but also, certainly, maintains a judiciary of high and the highest ranks, with the countless, indispensable retinue of attendants, clerks, gendarmes and other assistants, perhaps even executioners—I don't shrink from the word. And the purpose of this large organisation, gentlemen? It consists in arresting innocent people and instituting senseless proceedings against them, usually, as in my case, without result.
