Given the senselessness of the whole thing, how could the worst corruption among the officials be concealed? It's impossible; even the highest judge could not manage that for himself alone. That is why the guards try to steal the clothes off arrested people's backs, why supervisors break into other people's homes, why the innocent are to be humiliated before entire gatherings rather than questioned. The guards merely told me about storerooms where the arrested people's property is taken. I'd like to see those storage places, where the possessions they have worked so hard to acquire are rotting, insofar as they haven't been stolen by thieving storeroom officials.”

A shriek from the hall's far end interrupted K. He shaded his eyes to look that way, since the dull daylight whitened the haze and dazzled him. The washerwoman was involved, whose very entrance K. had recognised as a serious disruption. Whether she was now at fault could not be made out. All K. could see was a man who had drawn her into a corner beside the door and was pressing her to him. The shrieking came from him, though, not her: his mouth was stretched wide and his gaze directed at the ceiling. A little circle had formed round the pair. Those nearby in the gallery seemed delighted at this interruption of the seriousness K. had brought into the gathering. His first impulse was to run over, and he also thought everybody would want to restore order there and at least eject the pair from the hall. Yet the front ranks ahead of him stood firm; nobody moved or allowed him through. On the contrary, they obstructed him. A hand—he lacked time to turn and see whose—gripped his collar from behind, while old men held their arms out. The couple scarcely occupied his thoughts any longer; he felt his liberty being curtailed, felt that the arrest was now becoming serious, and jumped heedlessly down from the platform. He now confronted the throng eye to eye. Had his judgment of these people been wrong? Had he credited his address with too much influence? Had their behaviour been an act all through his speech, an act they now tired of as his conclusions approached? The faces surrounding him! Tiny black eyes darted about, cheeks sagged like drunkards', and long beards stood stiff and sparse: fingers thrust into them seemed merely to form claws, rather than to grasp beards at all. Beneath those beards, however—and this was K.'s real discovery—badges of various colours and sizes gleamed on coat collars. As far as he could see, everybody wore them. All belonged together, the apparent parties on both sides; turning suddenly, he saw identical badges on the examining magistrate's collar as the man sat calmly looking down, his hands in his lap. “So!” K. cried, throwing up his arms; his sudden insight demanded room. “Officials, every one of you, I see! You are the corrupt gang I have been speaking against. You crowded in here as listeners and spies, pretended to form parties, with one applauding to put me to the test; you wanted a lesson in misleading the innocent. Well, I trust your presence here has proved thoroughly useless. Either you have amused yourselves because somebody expected you to defend innocence, or else”—“Let go or I'll hit you!” K. shouted at a trembling old man who had pushed particularly close—“or else you really have learned something. With that, I wish you luck in your trade.” He swiftly picked up his hat from the table's edge and forced his way towards the exit amid universal silence, certainly the silence of utter astonishment. The examining magistrate seemed to have been quicker still, since he was waiting at the door. “One moment,” he said. K. stopped, looking past the magistrate at the door, whose handle was already in his grasp. “I merely wanted to point out,” the magistrate said, “that today you have deprived yourself—though you may not yet realise it—of the advantage questioning invariably offers an arrested person.” K. laughed towards the door. “You scoundrels, keep all your questioning!” he cried, opened it and hurried downstairs. Behind him the gathering's noise rose again as it revived and began discussing the events in the manner of students.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Throughout the following week K. waited each day for another notification. He could not believe his renunciation of questioning had been taken literally, and when by Sunday evening the expected notification had indeed failed to arrive, he assumed he had been tacitly summoned again to the same building at the same hour. He returned accordingly on Sunday, taking the stairs and corridors without detours this time. Greetings came from the doorways of several people who recognised him. He had no further need to ask his way, and quickly arrived at the right entrance. The door opened the moment he knocked. Leaving the woman he knew standing in the doorway without another glance, he made directly for the room beyond. “There is no sitting today,” she told him. “Why shouldn't there be a sitting?” he asked, unwilling to believe it. Opening the next room's door, the woman convinced him. It was genuinely empty, and emptiness made it look even more wretched than last Sunday. A few books lay on the table, which stood unchanged on the platform. “May I look through those books?” K. asked, less from particular curiosity than from a wish not to have come entirely in vain. “No,” the woman said, closing the door again. “That isn't permitted. They are the examining magistrate's books.” “I see,” K. said with a nod. “Presumably legal textbooks; and with this kind of judicial system it is customary to condemn people not merely in innocence but in ignorance as well.” “I suppose so,” said the woman, who had not quite followed him. “Then I'll be going,” K. replied. “Is there anything I should tell the examining magistrate?” she asked. “You know him?” K. asked. “Naturally. My husband is a court attendant.” Only now did K. notice that the room, previously containing nothing but a washtub, was now a fully furnished living room. Observing his surprise, she explained: “Yes, we live here rent-free, but on days when the court sits we must clear the room. My husband's position has its drawbacks.” “It isn't the room that surprises me so much,” K. said, looking at her angrily, “as your being married.” “Perhaps you mean the incident at the last sitting, when I interrupted your speech?” she asked. “Naturally,” K. replied. “By today it is over and almost forgotten, but at the time it positively enraged me. And now you yourself tell me you're married.” “Having your speech broken off did you no harm. It was judged very unfavourably afterwards, too.” “Possibly,” K. said, diverting the subject, “but that is no excuse for you.” “Anybody who knows me excuses me,” she replied. “The man embracing me then has pursued me for a long time. I may not generally be attractive, but to him I am. There is no protection against it; even my husband has resigned himself. He must tolerate it to keep his position, because the man is a student and will probably acquire greater power. He is forever after me; he left only just before you arrived.” “That accords with everything else,” K. said. “It doesn't surprise me.” “You want to improve things here, perhaps?” she asked slowly, testing her words as though they might endanger both herself and K. “I gathered that from your speech, which I personally liked very much. Admittedly I heard only part. The opening escaped me; by the closing words the student and I were lying on the floor.—How repulsive it is here,” she added, pausing before she took his hand. “Do you think you can bring about an improvement?” Smiling, K. turned his hand a little within her soft hands. “Strictly speaking,” he replied, “I haven't been appointed to bring about improvements here, as you call it. If you told the examining magistrate that, for example, you would be laughed at or punished. In fact I certainly wouldn't have involved myself voluntarily in these matters; this judicial system's need of improvement would never have cost me any sleep. But the arrest supposedly made upon me—I am arrested, you see—has forced me to intervene for my own sake. If in doing so I can be useful to you as well, I shall naturally be very glad. Not merely from benevolence: you, too, can help me.” “How could I possibly do that?” she asked. “By showing me, for instance, the books on that table now.” “Of course!” she cried, hastily pulling him after her. The books were old and much handled. One cover was almost broken across its middle, its pieces held together only by fibres. “Everything here is so filthy,” K. said, shaking his head. Before he could reach for the books she wiped off the dust with her apron, superficially at least. Opening the first volume, he found an indecent illustration. A naked woman and a naked man sat on a sofa; the artist's vulgar intention was unmistakable, but his ineptitude was so great that in the end one saw merely two figures protruding too bodily from the picture, sitting excessively upright, and turning towards each other only with difficulty because the perspective was wrong. K. turned no further pages, opening only the title page of the second volume. This was a novel called “The Torments Grete Suffered at the Hands of Her Husband Hans.” “These are the legal books studied here,” K. said. “People like these are to judge me.” “I will help you,” the woman said. “Will you let me?” “Could you really, without endangering yourself? You said just now how dependent your husband was on his superiors.” “Nevertheless I want to help,” she answered. “Come, we must discuss it. Say no more about my danger; I fear danger only where I choose to. Come.” Indicating the platform, she invited him to sit beside her on its step. “Your dark eyes are beautiful,” she said once they were seated, looking up into his face. “They tell me mine are beautiful too, but yours are much more so. I noticed them immediately when you first came in that day. They were also why I later came into the meeting room, something I never ordinarily do, and am even, in a way, forbidden to do.” So that is all it amounts to, K. thought. She is offering herself to me, corrupt like everybody here. She has had enough of the court officials, understandably, and therefore greets any stranger at all with a compliment about his eyes. He rose without speaking, as if he had uttered his thoughts aloud and thereby explained his behaviour to her. “I doubt you could help me,” he said. “Effective help would require connections with senior officials. You surely know only the subordinate employees swarming about here. No doubt you know them very well and could obtain a good deal from them; I don't dispute it. But the greatest concession obtainable from them would have no bearing whatever on the case's ultimate outcome. You, meanwhile, would have lost some friends. That is not what I want. Continue your existing relations with these people; they seem indispensable to you. I say this with some regret, because, to return your compliment in some fashion, I too find you very appealing, especially when you look at me so sadly, as now, though you have no reason whatever for sadness. You belong to the company I must fight against, yet are quite comfortable within it; you even love the student, or, if not love, at least prefer him to your husband. Your own words made that plain enough.” “No!” she cried. Remaining seated, she caught at his hand before he could withdraw it. “Don't leave now; you mustn't go away thinking wrongly of me. Could you really bring yourself to go now? Am I so worthless that you won't even grant me a little more of your time here?” “You misunderstand,” K. said, sitting down. “If my staying truly matters to you, I am happy to stay. I have time, after all; I came expecting a hearing today. What I said before was simply a request that you undertake nothing on my behalf in the case. Even that needn't offend you, when you consider that its outcome is of no concern to me and I shall merely laugh at a conviction. That assumes a genuine conclusion will ever be reached in the case—something I regard as highly doubtful. I think instead that through the officials' idleness, forgetfulness, or perhaps even fear, the proceedings have already been abandoned or soon will be. Of course it is also possible they will pretend to pursue the case in hope of some substantial bribe; quite fruitlessly, as I can tell them already, because nobody is getting a bribe from me. You could nevertheless do me one favour: tell the examining magistrate, or anybody else fond of circulating important news, that no trick, however plentifully these gentlemen are supplied with them, will ever induce me to bribe anyone. The prospect is utterly hopeless; you may tell them that openly. Perhaps they have realised it already, however, and even if they haven't, I care little whether they learn it now. It would merely spare the gentlemen some work, and admittedly spare me some inconveniences too, but I gladly accept those if I know each is simultaneously a blow against the others. And I intend to ensure that it is. Do you actually know the examining magistrate?” “Of course,” she said. “He was even the first person I thought of when offering to help. I didn't know he was only a minor official, but since you say so it is probably true. Even so, I believe the report he submits to those above him carries some influence. Reports pour from his pen. You say the officials are idle; that certainly doesn't apply to everyone, and especially not to this magistrate, who writes so much. Take last Sunday: the sitting went on almost until evening. Everybody else departed, but he remained in the hall and I had to supply a lamp. I could offer only my small kitchen lamp. It satisfied him, though, and he started writing at once. Meanwhile my husband had returned—he happened to have leave that Sunday—and we fetched the furniture and set up our room again. Neighbours came over later and we talked by candlelight; in short, we forgot the examining magistrate and went to bed. Suddenly in the night—it must have been very late—I woke to find him standing beside the bed, shielding the lamp with his hand so that no light should fall on my husband. An unnecessary precaution: my husband sleeps so soundly that even the light wouldn't have woken him. I was so frightened I almost screamed, but the magistrate was very kind. He urged caution and whispered that he had been writing until then, that he was returning the lamp, and that he would never forget the sight of me as he had found me asleep. All this was merely to tell you that he really does write many reports, particularly about you, since your questioning was certainly among the principal subjects of that two-day sitting. Reports of such length can't be wholly without significance. Besides, the incident shows that the examining magistrate is courting me; precisely now, in these early days—he must only just have noticed me at all—I may have considerable influence over him. I have further proof now of how much I matter to him. Yesterday he sent silk stockings as a present through the student, whom he trusts greatly and who works with him, supposedly for my cleaning the meeting room. That is just a pretext, though, since the work is my duty and my husband is paid for it. They are fine stockings, look”—she stretched out her legs, raised her skirts to her knees and examined the stockings herself—“fine stockings, but really too fine, and unsuitable for me.”

Abruptly she broke off, laid her hand over K.'s as if to reassure him, and whispered: “Quiet—Bertold is watching.” K. slowly raised his eyes. A young man stood in the meeting room's doorway, short, with legs that were not quite straight, trying to lend himself dignity by means of a short, sparse, reddish beard through which his fingers constantly moved. K. regarded him with curiosity. This was, after all, the first student of that unknown jurisprudence whom he had encountered on something like a human footing, a man who would probably also rise one day to senior office. The student, by contrast, appeared to ignore K. altogether. He merely beckoned to the woman with a finger briefly withdrawn from his beard, then went to the window. Leaning towards K., the woman whispered: “Please, please don't be angry with me or think ill of me. I have to go to him now, that horrible man—just look at his crooked legs. I shall be back in a moment, though, and afterwards, if you will take me along, I shall accompany you. Choose the destination yourself; do with me whatever pleases you. Being away from this place would make me happy—the longer the better, and best of all for ever.” After another stroke of K.'s hand she sprang up and ran to the window. Involuntarily he reached for her hand again, grasping empty air. She really did tempt him, and however much he reflected he found no sound reason to resist the temptation. A passing objection—that she was trapping him for the court—was easily dismissed. How could she trap him? Did he not always remain free enough to smash the entire court at once, at least insofar as it concerned him? Could he not trust himself that little? Moreover, her offer of help sounded sincere and might have value. Perhaps, too, no revenge on the examining magistrate and his adherents could be better than taking this woman away from them for himself. One night, after laboriously composing lying reports about K., the magistrate might then discover her bed empty. Her bed would be empty because she was his, because the woman now standing at that window—the full, pliant, warm body inside that dark garment of heavy, coarse material—was K.'s and nobody else's.

Having disposed of his objections to the woman in this way, he found the whispered conversation at the window too prolonged and rapped on the platform with his knuckles, then with his fist as well. The student glanced briefly towards K. over her shoulder but refused to be disturbed; indeed he pressed closer and put his arms round her. She lowered her head deeply as if listening attentively. As she bent, he gave her a loud kiss on the neck without appreciably interrupting his speech. To K. this confirmed the tyranny she had complained the student exercised over her. He rose and paced the room, casting sideways looks towards the student and considering how to get rid of him most quickly. It was therefore not unwelcome when the student, evidently bothered by K.'s pacing, which had at times become actual stamping, observed: “Impatient people can leave. You could have left earlier, too; nobody would have missed you. In fact you ought to have left immediately when I arrived, and wasted no time about it.” However much anger found expression in that remark, it also contained a future court official's arrogance towards an unwelcome defendant. Stopping almost against him, K. smiled and replied: “Impatient I certainly am. Your departure would be the simplest remedy for that impatience, though. If you came to study, however—I hear you are a student—I will gladly make room by leaving with the woman. You still have a great deal of studying ahead before becoming a judge, incidentally. I don't yet know your judicial system particularly well, but I assume crude talk alone, which you already manage with shameless skill, falls far short of what is needed.” “Letting him roam so freely was a mistake,” the student told the woman, as though explaining K.'s insulting speech to her. “I told the examining magistrate so. Between questionings they should at least have confined him to his room. Sometimes the magistrate is incomprehensible.” “Pointless talk,” K. said, extending his hand towards the woman. “Come along.” “Oh, I see,” the student said. “No, no, you aren't getting her.” With unexpected strength he lifted her onto one arm and ran for the door, his back bent, gazing tenderly up at her. Some fear of K. was unmistakable, yet he still dared provoke him, stroking and squeezing her arm with his free hand. For a few paces K. ran beside him, ready to seize him and, if necessary, throttle him. Then the woman said: “It is no use; the examining magistrate has sent for me. I cannot go with you. This little monster”—she passed a hand across the student's face—“this little monster won't let me.” “So you refuse to be released!” cried K. His hand came down on the young man's shoulder, and the student tried to bite it. “No!” she cried, warding K. off with both hands. “No, no, anything but that! What can you be thinking? It would ruin me. Leave him alone, please, please leave him. He is merely carrying out the magistrate's order and taking me to him.” “Then let him run, and let me never see you again,” K. said, furious with disappointment. He shoved the student's back, making him briefly stumble; a moment later, delighted not to have fallen, the student bounded all the higher with his burden. Following at a slow pace, he understood that these people had now beaten him for the first time beyond any possibility of doubt. Naturally this need not frighten him: only his seeking a fight had brought the defeat upon him. At home, pursuing his ordinary life, his superiority over every one of these people would be thousandfold; a kick would suffice to clear any of them from his way. He imagined the most ludicrous possible scene: this pitiable student, for instance, this puffed-up child, this crooked-legged wearer of a beard, kneeling before Elsa's bed with folded hands, begging for mercy. K. enjoyed the picture so much that he resolved to take the student to Elsa sometime, should any opportunity arise.

Curiosity sent K. hurrying to the doorway once more. He wanted to see where she was being carried; surely the student would not carry her through the streets in his arms. Their route proved much shorter. Directly opposite the flat's entrance a narrow wooden stairway led up, probably to the attic, turning so that its end was hidden. The student was carrying her up these stairs, now very slowly and with groans, exhausted by his running so far. The woman waved down to K. and tried, by raising and lowering her shoulders, to convey that she bore no blame for being abducted; the gesture contained little regret, however. K. looked at her without expression, as at a stranger, unwilling to reveal either his disappointment or how easily he could overcome it.

The pair had vanished, but K. still stood in the doorway. He had to suppose that she had not only betrayed him but lied as well in claiming she was being carried to the examining magistrate. Surely the magistrate would not be sitting in an attic waiting. Staring at the wooden stairs, however long one did it, explained nothing. Then K. noticed a small notice beside the stairs, crossed over, and read, in an unpractised, childish hand: “Stairs to the court offices.” So the court offices were up here in this tenement's attic? Such an establishment could hardly inspire much respect. For a defendant it was reassuring to imagine the court's limited funds, if it housed its offices where the tenants, themselves among the poorest, threw their useless rubbish. Of course the possibility remained that money was plentiful but the officials fell upon it before any could be spent on court purposes. In K.'s experience so far that was even highly probable. Such dilapidation, though degrading to a defendant, would then be fundamentally still more reassuring than the court's poverty. Now K. also understood why, for the first questioning, they were ashamed to summon a defendant to an attic and preferred to trouble him in his lodgings. What a position K. occupied in relation to this judge sitting in the attic, while he himself had a large room and an anteroom at the bank, and could look down through an immense pane of glass onto the busy city square! Admittedly he had no supplementary income from bribes or embezzlement, nor could he have an attendant carry a woman into his office. But those were things K. was quite happy to forgo, at least in this life.

While K. remained beside the notice, a man climbed the stairs and peered into the living room through its open doorway, which afforded a view into the meeting room too; eventually he asked if K. had recently noticed a woman here. “You must be the court attendant?” K. asked. “Yes,” the man replied. “Oh, and you are K., the defendant. Now I recognise you too. Welcome.” Quite unexpectedly, he offered K. his hand. When K. said nothing, the attendant added: “But no sitting has been announced for today.” “I know,” K. replied, studying the attendant's civilian coat. Its only official insignia were two gilt buttons beside several ordinary ones; they appeared to have been cut off an old military officer's greatcoat. “I spoke with your wife a short while ago. She has gone. The student carried her to the examining magistrate.” “You see,” the attendant said, “they're always carrying her away from me. Today is Sunday, and no work is required of me, but they send me off with a useless message solely to get me out of here. They don't even send me far: just far enough for me to hope that by hurrying I may return in time. So I run as hard as I can, shout my message through the crack of the door at the office I have been sent to, so breathless that they can hardly have understood, then run back. But the student has hurried even more than I have; admittedly his route was shorter, as he only needed to run down the attic stairs. If I weren't so dependent, I'd have crushed him against this wall long ago. Here, beside the notice. I dream of it constantly: pinned a little above the floor, arms extended, fingers spread, his crooked legs curled into a circle, and blood spattered all around. So far, though, it has remained a dream.” “No other remedy?” K. asked, smiling. “None that I know of,” the attendant answered. “And now it's getting worse. Until now he only carried her to his own quarters; now he takes her to the examining magistrate as well, something I have admittedly expected for a long time.” “Does your wife bear none of the blame?” K. asked; he had to restrain himself in asking, so strongly did he too now feel jealousy. “Certainly she does,” the attendant said. “Most of the blame, in fact. She attached herself to him. As for him, he pursues every woman. In this building alone he has already been thrown out of five flats into which he had sneaked. My wife is admittedly the prettiest woman here, and I of all people am forbidden to defend myself.” “If that is the situation, there is indeed no remedy,” K. said. “Why shouldn't there be?” the attendant asked. “Someone need only thrash that coward of a student once, when he tries to touch my wife, so thoroughly that he never dares again. I am not allowed to, though, and others won't oblige me because everyone fears his power. Only someone such as you could do it.” “Why me?” K. asked in surprise. “Because you are accused,” the attendant replied. “Yes,” K. said, “but that gives me all the more reason to fear his influence, probably over the preliminary investigation even if not over the outcome of the case.” “Yes, certainly,” the attendant said, as though K.'s view was exactly as valid as his own. “But as a rule we don't conduct hopeless cases here.” “I disagree,” K. said, “though that needn't prevent me from attending to the student when the occasion arises.” “I should be most grateful,” the attendant replied somewhat formally; he did not, after all, seem to believe that his greatest wish could be fulfilled. “Perhaps,” K. went on, “others among your officials, perhaps even all of them, deserve the same treatment.” “Yes, yes,” said the attendant, as if this were self-evident. Then he looked at K. with a trustfulness absent until now despite his friendliness, adding: “One is always rebelling, after all.” Yet the conversation seemed to have grown a little uncomfortable for him, because he cut it short: “I must report to the office now. Would you like to accompany me?” “I have no business there,” K. said. “You could look round the offices. Nobody will bother about you.” “Are they worth a visit?” K. asked hesitantly, though greatly inclined to go. “Well,” the attendant said, “I thought they might interest you.” “Very well,” K. finally replied, “I'll come.” He ran up the stairs faster than the attendant.

On entering he nearly fell, for another step lay just inside the door. “They show little consideration for the public,” he said. “None at all,” the attendant replied. “Just look at the waiting room here.” A long passage extended before them, with roughly constructed wooden doors opening into the attic's separate sections. Although it received no direct light, it was not wholly dark: some sections, instead of solid plank walls towards the passage, had only wooden lattice partitions, admittedly reaching the ceiling, through which a little light penetrated. Through them individual officials could also be seen writing at tables, or standing right against the lattice to watch people in the passage through its gaps. Only a few people occupied the passage, probably because it was Sunday. They made a very humble impression. At almost regular intervals they sat along two rows of long wooden benches lining its sides. All were shabbily dressed, although most belonged to the upper classes, judging from their expressions, bearing, styles of beard and many small details too elusive to specify. With no coat hooks available, they had placed their hats beneath the bench, probably following one another's example. Those seated nearest the entrance rose in greeting when they saw K. and the attendant. Seeing this, the next people thought they too must greet them, so everybody rose as the two passed. They never straightened completely; backs bent and knees flexed, they stood like beggars in the street. K. waited for the attendant, who was a little behind him, and remarked: “How humiliated they must be.” “Yes,” said the attendant. “They are defendants. Every person you see here is a defendant.” “Really!” K. said. “Then they are my colleagues.” He turned towards the nearest, a tall, slender man whose hair was already almost grey. “What are you waiting for here?” he politely asked. The unexpected address confused the man, all the more painfully to behold because he was evidently worldly and experienced, somebody who elsewhere surely knew how to maintain his composure and would not lightly surrender the superiority he had acquired over many others. Here, however, he could not answer so simple a question. He looked at the others as though they owed him assistance and, without it, nobody could require an answer of him. The attendant came up and tried to reassure and encourage him: “This gentleman only wants to know what you are waiting for. Please answer.” The attendant's voice, probably familiar to him, proved more effective. “I am waiting—” he began, then faltered. Evidently he had chosen that opening to correspond precisely to the question, but could now find no continuation. Several waiting people had come closer and surrounded the group. The attendant told them: “Move away, move away; leave the passage clear.” They retreated a little, though not to their former seats. Meanwhile the man being questioned had collected himself and even replied with a slight smile: “A month ago I submitted several applications for evidence to be taken in my case, and I am awaiting their disposal.” “You seem to be taking a great deal of trouble,” K. observed. “Yes,” the man answered. “It is my case, after all.” “Not everybody shares your view,” K. said. “I, for instance, am also accused, yet as I hope for salvation I have neither applied for evidence to be taken nor done anything else of the kind. Do you consider it necessary?” “I can't say for certain,” the man replied, wholly uncertain once more. He apparently thought K. was joking with him, and probably, fearing another mistake, would have preferred simply to repeat his earlier answer. But under K.'s impatient gaze he said only: “In my own case, I have submitted applications for evidence.” “Perhaps you disbelieve that I am accused?” K. asked. “Oh, please, certainly,” the man said, stepping slightly aside. His answer conveyed fear rather than belief. “So you don't believe me?” K. asked, taking his arm, unconsciously prompted by the man's submissiveness, as though trying to compel belief. He had no wish to hurt him and had touched him only very lightly; nevertheless the man cried out as though K. had gripped him with red-hot tongs instead of two fingers. This ridiculous outcry exhausted K.'s patience altogether. If they did not believe he was accused, so much the better; perhaps the man even took him for a judge. This time he gripped him more firmly in parting, pushed him back onto the bench and continued on his way. “Most defendants are sensitive like that,” the attendant said. Behind them nearly all those waiting now gathered about the man, who had stopped crying out, and seemed to question him closely about the incident. A guard approached K., identifiable chiefly by a sabre whose scabbard, to judge at least by its colour, was aluminium. This astonished K. so much that he even reached towards it. The guard had come because of the outcry and asked what had happened. The attendant tried a few reassuring words, but the guard declared that he must still investigate for himself, saluted, and continued with exceedingly quick yet tiny steps, probably measured out by gout.

K. gave little further thought to the guard or the company in the passage, particularly as about halfway along he saw a chance to turn right through an opening without a door. He checked with the attendant that this was the proper route; the attendant nodded, and K. made the turn. Having always to walk a pace or two ahead annoyed him: in this place, at least, it might look as though he were being brought in under arrest. He therefore often waited for the attendant, only for the man to lag again immediately. At last, to end his discomfort, K. said: “Now I've seen the place. I'd like to leave.” “You haven't seen everything yet,” the attendant said quite innocently. “Everything isn't what I want to see,” K. replied, genuinely tired now. “I want to go. Which way is out?” “Surely you aren't lost already?” the attendant asked in surprise. “Continue to that corner, turn right along the passage, and go straight to the door.” “Accompany me,” K. said. “Show me the route; I'll miss it. There are so many ways here.” “There is only one way,” the attendant replied, now reproachfully. “I can't go back again with you. I have my report to deliver and have already lost a great deal of time on your account.” “Accompany me,” K. repeated more sharply, as if he had finally caught the attendant in a lie. “Don't shout,” the man whispered. “We are surrounded by offices. If you refuse to go back alone, come a little further with me, or wait here while I deliver my report; afterwards I will gladly walk back with you.” “No, no,” K. said. “Waiting is out of the question. You must accompany me now.” He had not yet looked about the space he was in; only when one of the many surrounding wooden doors opened did he turn his eyes towards it. A girl entered, probably attracted by his loud voice, and asked: “What does the gentleman require?” Beyond her another man could be seen approaching from a distance through the half-light. K. looked at the attendant. Hadn't he said nobody would trouble about him? Here were two already. It would take little for the officials to notice him and demand an explanation for his presence. The only comprehensible and acceptable explanation would be that, as a defendant, he wanted the date of his next questioning. That was precisely the explanation he refused to give, especially as it would be untrue. Mere curiosity had brought him, or, still less admissible as an explanation, a wish to establish that this judicial system's interior was as repulsive as its exterior. His assumption did indeed seem correct. He wished to penetrate no further; what he had already seen oppressed him sufficiently. At present he was in no condition to face a senior official, who might emerge from any doorway. He wanted to leave—with the attendant, or alone if necessary.

But standing there silently must have looked remarkable, and indeed the girl and the attendant watched as though some great transformation might overtake him in the next minute and they were determined not to miss it. The man K. had noticed earlier in the distance stood in the doorway, holding its low lintel and rocking slightly on tiptoe like an impatient spectator. First to understand the cause of K.'s behaviour—a slight indisposition—was the girl. Fetching an armchair, she asked whether he wanted to sit. K. sat down immediately and, for firmer support, rested his elbows on its arms. “A little dizzy, are you?” she asked. Her face was now close before him, wearing the severe expression some women have in the very bloom of youth. “Don't worry about it,” she said. “It's quite ordinary here. Almost everybody has an attack on their first visit. Is this your first? Well then, there's nothing unusual about it. The sun beats on the roof timbers, and the heated wood makes the air heavy and stale. That makes this place rather unsuitable for offices, however great its other advantages. As for the air, on days when many people attend—and that means almost every day—it becomes scarcely breathable. When you consider, too, how much washing is hung here to dry—we cannot forbid the tenants altogether—you'll no longer be surprised at feeling a little ill. Eventually one becomes perfectly accustomed to the air, though. On your second or third visit you'll hardly notice the oppressiveness. Are you feeling any better yet?” K. made no reply. This sudden weakness, leaving him at these people's mercy, embarrassed him too much. Besides, learning the causes of his sickness had made him a little worse rather than better. The girl noticed immediately. Seeking to give him some relief, she picked up the hook-ended pole resting by the wall and used it to open a little outside hatch immediately over his head. So much soot fell through, however, that she had to close it straight away and clean his hands with her handkerchief; K. was too tired to do it himself. He would gladly have sat quietly until strong enough to leave, and that would have happened sooner if they paid him less attention. Instead, the girl added: “You cannot stay here; we're obstructing the traffic”—K.'s eyes asked what traffic he could possibly be obstructing here—“I can take you to the sickroom, if you like.” Turning to the man in the doorway, she said, “Please help me”; he approached at once. But the sickroom was the last place K. wanted. Being led further in was precisely what he wished to avoid: the deeper he went, the worse it must become. “I'm able to walk now,” he therefore said, rising unsteadily, spoiled by the comfort of sitting. Once up, however, he could not remain upright. Shaking his head, he admitted, “After all, it can't be done,” and sighed as he sat once more. He thought of the attendant: despite everything, getting K. outside would be easy for him. Apparently, however, he had long since gone. K. peered between the girl and the man standing before him without finding him.

“I believe,” said the man—who was elegantly dressed, particularly notable for a grey waistcoat ending in two long, sharply cut points—“that this gentleman's indisposition results from the atmosphere here. It would therefore be best, and most agreeable to him, if instead of taking him to the sickroom we took him right out of the offices.” “Exactly!” K. cried, almost interrupting him in his delight. “I shall certainly recover immediately. I'm not particularly weak, either; a little support beneath the arms is all I require. I won't cause you much trouble, and the distance isn't great. Just take me to the door; I can sit on the steps a little afterwards and shall soon be recovered. Attacks like this are quite foreign to me; I'm surprised myself. I too am an office worker, accustomed to office air, but here it seems excessive, as you yourself say. So would you kindly guide me a little? I feel dizzy and sick whenever I stand without help.” His shoulders lifted, offering them easier access to support him beneath the arms.

The man did not respond to this invitation, however, but kept his hands motionless in his trouser pockets and laughed loudly. “There,” he told the girl, “I did identify it correctly. Only this place makes the gentleman ill; he isn't generally unwell.” The girl smiled as well, but tapped his arm lightly with her fingertips, as if his joke at K.'s expense had gone too far. “Whatever do you suppose?” the man continued, still laughing. “I really do intend to take him out.” “Then that's all right,” she said, inclining her delicate head momentarily. “You shouldn't read too much into that laugh,” she told K. He was staring ahead sadly again, apparently in no need of an explanation. “This gentleman—if introductions are permissible?” A gesture from the man granted permission. “Here you have our information officer. He supplies the people waiting here with all the information they need; since our judicial system is little known among the population, there is a great demand for information. He can answer every question. You may test him sometime, if you like. But that isn't his sole merit. A second is his elegant dress. We—that is, the officials—once felt that the information officer, who deals constantly with people attending court and is their first contact, should be smartly dressed to make a dignified first impression. Unfortunately the other officials dress poorly and behind the times; my own appearance will show you that. Expenditure on clothing hardly seems worthwhile when we are in these offices almost without interruption and even sleep here. For the officer providing information, however, we decided, as I mentioned, that a fine wardrobe was essential. Our administration is rather peculiar on this point and wouldn't supply them, so we took up a collection—people attending court contributed too—and bought him this fine suit and others as well. Everything is now arranged for a good impression, only he spoils it again with his laughter and frightens people.” “Quite so,” the gentleman said mockingly, “but, miss, why tell him all our intimate affairs—or rather force them on him, since he doesn't want to hear them? Just look at him sitting there, evidently preoccupied with his own concerns.” K. had no inclination even to contradict him. The girl's intention might be good, perhaps to distract him or allow him to collect himself, but her method was mistaken. “I had to explain your laughter,” she said. “It was insulting.” “I imagine he would pardon worse insults if in the end I got him outside.” K. remained silent, not even raising his eyes. He tolerated their discussing him like an object; indeed that suited him best. Suddenly, though, he felt the information officer's hand on one arm and the girl's on the other. “Up you get, then, you feeble fellow,” the information officer said. “My warmest thanks to you both,” K. replied, pleasantly surprised. He rose slowly, himself moving their hands to where he most needed support. “It looks,” the girl whispered into his ear as they approached the passage, “as though I'm particularly anxious to show the information officer in a favourable light. Let people think so; I want to speak the truth. His heart isn't hard. Taking sick people outside is no duty of his, yet he does it, as you see. Perhaps none of us is hardhearted; perhaps we'd all gladly help, but as court officials we easily appear hardhearted and unwilling to help anybody. I suffer from that quite badly.” “Wouldn't you care to sit awhile here?” the information officer asked. They had reached the passage and stood directly before the defendant K. had addressed earlier. K. was almost ashamed before him: earlier he had stood so erect, now he needed two people's support; the information officer balanced his hat on outspread fingers, and his disordered hair fell across his sweating forehead. The defendant seemed to notice none of it, however. He stood humbly before the information officer, who looked over him, and tried only to justify his presence. “I know,” he said, “that my applications cannot be disposed of today. Nevertheless I came, thinking I might wait here. It is Sunday, I have time, and I disturb nobody here.” “You needn't offer so much justification,” the information officer replied. “Your diligence is highly commendable. True, you occupy space here unnecessarily, but so long as it doesn't inconvenience me I certainly won't prevent you from keeping close track of your affair's progress. After seeing people who disgracefully neglect their duty, one learns patience with people like you. Be seated.” “How well he speaks to the people attending court,” the girl whispered. K. nodded, but started when the information officer asked him again: “Would you like a seat here?” “No,” K. said. “Resting is not what I want.” He spoke with all possible firmness, though sitting would in fact have helped him greatly. He felt as if seasick, as if aboard a ship in rough seas. Water seemed to crash against the wooden walls; from the passage's depths came a roar like breaking waves; the passage seemed to roll sideways, lifting and lowering the waiting people on either side. All the less could he understand how his two guides, the girl and the man, remained so composed. His fate lay entirely in their hands. If they released him he would topple like a plank. Keen glances darted from their small eyes. K. felt the regularity of their steps without taking them himself, for he was almost carried from one step to the next. Eventually he realised they were speaking to him, but could not make out their words. He heard only the noise filling everything, through which a steady high note seemed to sound, like a siren. “Louder,” he whispered, his head lowered, ashamed because he knew they had spoken loudly enough, though unintelligibly to him. Then finally fresh air swept towards him, as though a rent had opened in the wall ahead. Beside him came the words: “He wants to leave to begin with, but once he reaches the way out he stays rooted there, even after being told a hundred times.” K. realised he stood before the exit, its door opened by the girl. All his strength seemed to return at once. For a foretaste of freedom he immediately stepped onto a stair and from there took leave of his companions, who bent down towards him. Repeating his thanks, he shook both their hands again and again, stopping only when he thought he saw that, accustomed to the office atmosphere, they were having difficulty tolerating the comparatively fresh air rising from the stairs. They could scarcely reply, and the girl might have fallen had K. not closed the door extremely quickly. He then stood still a moment, used a pocket mirror to smooth his hair, and retrieved his hat from the next landing—the information officer must have thrown it there. Then he ran downstairs, so refreshed and taking such long bounds that the change almost frightened him. His normally robust health had never sprung such surprises on him before. Was his body about to revolt and prepare another case against him, since he bore the old one so effortlessly? He did not altogether reject the idea of consulting a doctor at the next opportunity. In any event—and here he could advise himself—he intended to spend all future Sunday mornings better than this one.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: For some time afterwards K. found it impossible to exchange even a few words with Miss Bürstner. He tried in all sorts of ways to approach her, but she always knew how to prevent it. He came home immediately after work, sat on the sofa in his room without turning on the light, and occupied himself with nothing but watching the entrance hall. If the maid happened to pass and closed the door of the apparently empty room, he got up after a little while and opened it again. In the mornings he rose an hour earlier than usual in the hope of meeting Miss Bürstner alone as she went to her office. But none of these attempts succeeded. Then he wrote her a letter, both to her office and to the apartment, in which he again sought to justify his behaviour, offered any form of redress, promised never to overstep whatever boundaries she set him, and asked only to be given the opportunity of speaking to her once, particularly since he could make no arrangements with Mrs Grubach until he had first consulted her. Finally he told her that the following Sunday he would wait in his room all day for some sign from her that offered the prospect of his request being granted, or at least explained why she could not grant it although he had promised to defer to her in everything. The letters were not returned, but no answer came either. On Sunday, however, there was a sign clear enough. Early in the morning K. noticed through the keyhole unusual activity in the entrance hall, which was soon explained. A teacher of French—she was in fact German and called Montag—a frail, pale young woman with a slight limp, who had until now occupied a room of her own, was moving into Miss Bürstner's room. For hours she could be seen shuffling through the entrance hall. There was always another piece of linen, a little cloth or a book that had been forgotten and had to be fetched specially and carried to the new accommodation.

When Mrs Grubach brought K. his breakfast—since she had angered him so much, she no longer left even the slightest service to the maid—he could not restrain himself from speaking to her for the first time. “Why is there such a noise in the entrance hall today?” he asked while pouring the coffee. “Couldn't it be stopped? Must the tidying be done on a Sunday?” Although K. did not look up at Mrs Grubach, he noticed her breathe as though in relief. Even these stern questions she took as forgiveness or the beginning of forgiveness. “There's no tidying going on, Mr K.,” she said. “Miss Montag is only moving in with Miss Bürstner and carrying her things over.” She said nothing more, but waited to see how K. would take it and whether he would allow her to go on. K., however, put her to the test, thoughtfully stirring his coffee with the spoon and remaining silent. Then he looked up at her and said: “Have you given up your earlier suspicions about Miss Bürstner yet?” “Mr K.!” exclaimed Mrs Grubach, who had been waiting only for this question, holding her clasped hands out towards him. “You took a casual remark so much to heart the other day. I never remotely intended to offend you or anyone else. You've known me long enough, Mr K., to be sure of that. You've no idea how I've suffered these last few days! Me, slander my lodgers! And you believed it, Mr K.! And you said I should give you notice! Give you notice!” The last cry was already choked with tears. She raised her apron to her face and sobbed aloud.

“Please don't cry, Mrs Grubach,” said K., looking out of the window. He was thinking only of Miss Bürstner and of her having taken another girl into her room. “Please don't cry,” he said again when he turned back into the room and Mrs Grubach was still crying. “I didn't mean it so badly then either. We simply misunderstood each other. That can happen even between old friends.” Mrs Grubach lowered her apron below her eyes to see whether K. was really reconciled. “Yes, that's how it is,” said K., and now, since her behaviour suggested that the captain had revealed nothing, he ventured to add: “Do you really think I could quarrel with you over a girl I hardly know?” “That's precisely it, Mr K.,” said Mrs Grubach. It was her misfortune that as soon as she felt at all freer she immediately said something clumsy. “I kept asking myself: Why does Mr K. take Miss Bürstner's side so strongly? Why does he quarrel with me over her, although he knows that every angry word from him robs me of sleep? After all, I've said nothing about the young lady except what I've seen with my own eyes.” K. said nothing to this; with his first word he would have had to drive her from the room, and he did not want to. He contented himself with drinking his coffee and making Mrs Grubach feel that she was superfluous. Outside they could again hear Miss Montag's dragging steps as she crossed the entire entrance hall. “Do you hear that?” K. asked, gesturing towards the door. “Yes,” said Mrs Grubach with a sigh. “I wanted to help her and have the maid help too, but she's stubborn; she wants to move everything herself. I'm surprised at Miss Bürstner. I often find it trying enough to have Miss Montag as a lodger, but Miss Bürstner is even taking her into her room.” “That needn't concern you at all,” said K., crushing the remaining sugar in his cup. “Does it cause you any loss?” “No,” said Mrs Grubach. “In itself it's quite welcome to me; it frees a room where I can put my nephew, the captain. I've been afraid for some time that he might have disturbed you these past few days, while I've had to let him stay next door in the living room. He isn't very considerate.” “What ideas you have!” said K., standing up. “There's no question of that. You seem to think I'm oversensitive because I can't endure these wanderings of Miss Montag's—there she goes back again.” Mrs Grubach felt quite powerless. “Shall I tell her to put off the rest of the move, Mr K.? If you wish, I'll do it at once.” “But she's supposed to move in with Miss Bürstner!” said K. “Yes,” said Mrs Grubach, not quite understanding what he meant. “Well, then,” said K., “she has to carry her things over.” Mrs Grubach merely nodded. This silent helplessness, outwardly indistinguishable from defiance, irritated K. still more. He began pacing between the window and the door, thereby depriving Mrs Grubach of the opportunity to leave, which she would otherwise probably have done.

K. had just reached the door again when there was a knock. It was the maid, reporting that Miss Montag would like a few words with Mr K. and therefore asked him to come to the dining room, where she was waiting. K. listened thoughtfully to the maid, then turned an almost mocking look on the startled Mrs Grubach. The look seemed to say that he had long foreseen this invitation from Miss Montag and that it fitted perfectly with the torment he was being made to endure that Sunday morning by Mrs Grubach's lodgers. He sent the maid back with the answer that he would come at once, then went to the wardrobe to change his jacket. In response to Mrs Grubach, who was quietly lamenting the troublesome woman, he merely asked her to take the breakfast things away. “But you've hardly touched anything,” said Mrs Grubach. “Oh, do take it away!” K. cried. He felt as though Miss Montag were somehow mixed into everything, making it repulsive.
As he crossed the entrance hall, he looked towards the closed door of Miss Bürstner's room. But he had not been invited there, only to the dining room, whose door he pulled open without knocking.

It was a very long but narrow room with one window. There was only enough space for two cupboards to stand at angles in the corners beside the door; all the rest was taken up by the long dining table, which began near the door and reached almost to the large window, making it virtually inaccessible. The table was already laid for a great many people, since almost all the lodgers ate their midday meal here on Sundays.

When K. came in, Miss Montag approached from the window along one side of the table. They greeted each other silently. Then Miss Montag, holding her head unusually high as always, said: “I don't know whether you know me.” K. looked at her with narrowed eyes. “Certainly,” he said. “You've been living with Mrs Grubach for quite some time.” “But I believe you don't take much interest in the boarding house,” said Miss Montag. “No,” said K. “Won't you sit down?” said Miss Montag. In silence they each drew out a chair at the far end of the table and sat facing one another. But Miss Montag immediately got up again, for she had left her handbag on the windowsill, and went to fetch it, dragging her way across the whole room. When she returned, lightly swinging the handbag, she said: “I only want to speak a few words to you on behalf of my friend. She wanted to come herself, but she's feeling a little unwell today. She asks you to excuse her and hear me in her place. She couldn't have told you anything different from what I shall tell you. On the contrary, I believe I can tell you even more, since I'm comparatively uninvolved. Don't you agree?”

“What is there to say?” replied K., tired of seeing Miss Montag's eyes constantly fixed on his lips. In this way she was already claiming authority over what he had yet to say. “Miss Bürstner evidently doesn't wish to grant me the private conversation I asked her for.” “That's it,” said Miss Montag, “or rather, that isn't it at all. You put it with peculiar sharpness. Generally speaking, conversations are neither granted nor refused. But people may consider a conversation unnecessary, and that is what has happened here. Now, after your remark, I can speak openly. You asked my friend, in writing or in person, for a conversation. My friend, however, knows—or so I must assume—what that conversation would concern, and for reasons I don't know she is therefore convinced that no one would benefit if it actually took place. Besides, she only told me about it yesterday and very briefly. She said then that it couldn't matter very much to you either, since the idea had occurred to you only by chance, and you would realise for yourself, without any special explanation, if not already then very soon, how pointless the whole thing was. I replied that that might be true, but that for complete clarity I would nevertheless consider it useful to send you an explicit answer. I offered to undertake the task, and after some hesitation my friend gave in to me. Now I hope I have acted in your interests too, because even the smallest uncertainty in the most trivial matter is always distressing, and if, as in this case, it can easily be removed, surely it is better to do so at once.” “Thank you,” K. said immediately, slowly standing up, looking at Miss Montag, then across the table, then out of the window—the house opposite stood in sunlight—and going towards the door. Miss Montag followed him a few paces, as though she did not quite trust him. But at the door both had to step back, for it opened and Captain Lanz entered. K. saw him close up for the first time. He was a tall man of about forty, with a sunburnt, fleshy face. He made a slight bow that included K., then went to Miss Montag and respectfully kissed her hand. His movements were very assured. His courtesy towards Miss Montag contrasted strikingly with K.'s treatment of her. Nevertheless, Miss Montag did not seem angry with K.; indeed, as K. thought he noticed, she even wanted to introduce him to the captain. But K. did not want to be introduced. He would have been incapable of showing any friendliness either to the captain or to Miss Montag. The kiss on her hand had joined them, in his eyes, into a group intent on keeping him away from Miss Bürstner under an appearance of the greatest innocence and selflessness. Yet K. believed he understood not only that; he also understood that Miss Montag had chosen a good, though double-edged, method. She exaggerated the importance of the relationship between Miss Bürstner and K., above all the importance of the requested conversation, while trying at the same time to make it seem that K. was the one exaggerating everything. She would be proved wrong. K. intended to exaggerate nothing; he knew that Miss Bürstner was a little typist who should not resist him for long. In this he deliberately took no account at all of what he had learnt about her from Mrs Grubach. He considered all this as he left the room with scarcely a farewell. He meant to go straight to his own room, but a small laugh from Miss Montag, which he heard behind him from the dining room, gave him the idea that perhaps he could surprise both her and the captain. He looked around and listened for any disturbance that might come from the surrounding rooms. All was quiet; only the conversation in the dining room could be heard, and Mrs Grubach's voice from the passage leading to the kitchen. The opportunity seemed favourable. K. went to Miss Bürstner's door and knocked softly. When nothing stirred, he knocked again, but still no answer came. Was she asleep? Or really unwell? Or was she merely pretending not to be there because she guessed that only K. could be knocking so softly? K. assumed she was pretending and knocked harder. Finally, since the knocking had no effect, he opened the door cautiously, not without the feeling that he was doing something wrong and, moreover, useless. No one was in the room. It scarcely resembled the room K. had known, either. Two beds now stood one behind the other along the wall; three chairs near the door were heaped with clothes and linen; a cupboard stood open. Miss Bürstner had probably gone out while Miss Montag was talking at K. in the dining room. He was not greatly dismayed by this. He had scarcely expected any longer to meet Miss Bürstner so easily; he had made this attempt almost solely in defiance of Miss Montag. All the more embarrassing, however, was the sight, as he closed the door again, of Miss Montag and the captain talking in the open doorway of the dining room. They might have been standing there ever since K. opened the door. They avoided any appearance of watching him, spoke quietly, and followed his movements only as people glance distractedly around during a conversation. Yet those looks weighed heavily on K., and he hurried along the wall to his own room.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: One of the following evenings, as K. passed along the corridor between his office and the main staircase—this time he was almost the last to go home; only two attendants were still working in the dispatch office, in the small pool of light cast by an electric bulb—he heard sighs coming from behind a door where he had always supposed there was nothing but a lumber room, though he had never seen inside it. He stopped in surprise and listened again to make sure he was not mistaken. For a little while there was silence, but then the sighs came again. At first he meant to fetch one of the attendants; a witness might be useful. But then such uncontrollable curiosity seized him that he positively flung the door open. As he had rightly supposed, it was a lumber room. Useless old printed forms and empty earthenware ink bottles lying on their sides were scattered just beyond the threshold. In the room itself, however, stood three men, stooping in the low space. A candle fixed to a shelf gave them light. “What are you doing here?” K. asked, stumbling over his words in his excitement, though not loudly. One man, who evidently dominated the others and drew the eye first, was encased in a kind of dark leather garment that left his neck bare far down his chest and his arms entirely exposed. He did not answer. But the other two cried: “Sir! We're to be flogged because you complained about us to the examining magistrate.” Only now did K. recognise that they really were the guards Franz and Willem, and that the third man held a rod with which to flog them. “Well,” said K., staring at them, “I didn't complain. I only said what happened in my apartment. And your behaviour certainly wasn't beyond reproach.” “Sir,” said Willem, while Franz apparently sought protection from the third man behind him, “if you knew how badly we're paid, you'd judge us more kindly. I have a family to feed, and Franz here wanted to get married. One tries to make money however one can; work alone won't do it, even the hardest work. Your fine linen tempted me. Of course guards are forbidden to act like that; it was wrong, but it's traditional for the linen to belong to the guards. It's always been that way, believe me. And it's understandable: what do such things still mean to someone unfortunate enough to be arrested? But if he then brings it up in public, punishment has to follow.” “I didn't know what you've just told me, and I certainly didn't demand your punishment. I was concerned with a principle.” “Franz,” Willem said, turning to the other guard, “didn't I tell you the gentleman hadn't demanded our punishment? Now you hear that he didn't even know we had to be punished.” “Don't let speeches like that move you,” the third man said to K. “The punishment is as just as it is unavoidable.” “Don't listen to him,” said Willem, interrupting himself only to bring quickly to his mouth the hand that had just received a stroke of the rod. “We're only being punished because you reported us. Otherwise nothing would have happened to us, even if they'd found out what we'd done. Can that be called justice? We two, but especially I, had proved ourselves as guards over a long period—you yourself must admit that, from the authority's point of view, we guarded you well—we had prospects of advancement and would certainly soon have become floggers ourselves, like this man, who merely had the good fortune that no one reported him, because such a report is really very rare. And now, sir, everything is lost. Our careers are over; we'll have to do work far more subordinate than guarding, and on top of that we're now to receive this terribly painful flogging.” “Can the rod hurt so much?” K. asked, examining the rod the flogger swung in front of him. “We'll have to strip completely naked,” said Willem. “Oh, I see,” said K., looking closely at the flogger. He was sunburnt like a sailor and had a wild, fresh face. “Isn't there any way to spare these two the flogging?” he asked him. “No,” said the flogger, shaking his head with a smile. “Undress,” he ordered the guards. To K. he said: “You mustn't believe everything they tell you. Fear of the beating has already made them a little feeble-minded. What this one, for instance”—he pointed at Willem—“said about his possible career is downright ridiculous. Look how fat he is; the first strokes will be lost in the fat altogether. Do you know what made him so fat? He's in the habit of eating every arrested person's breakfast. Didn't he eat yours too? Well, just as I said. But a man with a belly like that can never, ever become a flogger. It's quite out of the question.” “There are floggers like that too,” Willem insisted, as he undid his trouser belt. “No,” said the flogger, drawing the rod across his neck so that he flinched. “You're supposed to be undressing, not listening.” “I'd reward you well if you let them go,” said K., taking out his wallet without looking at the flogger again; such transactions were best conducted with lowered eyes on both sides. “So you can report me too,” said the flogger, “and have me flogged as well. No, no!” “Be sensible,” said K. “If I'd wanted these two punished, I wouldn't now want to buy their freedom. I could simply slam this door, refuse to see or hear anything more and go home. But I'm not doing that. On the contrary, I'm seriously concerned to free them. If I'd suspected they were to be punished, or could even be punished, I would never have mentioned their names. I don't consider them guilty at all. The organisation is guilty; the senior officials are guilty.” “That's right!” the guards cried, and immediately received a stroke across their already bare backs. “If you had a high-ranking judge here under your rod,” said K., pressing down the rod, which was already about to rise again, as he spoke, “I certainly wouldn't stop you from striking. On the contrary, I'd give you money to strengthen you in a good cause.” “What you say sounds believable,” said the flogger, “but I don't take bribes. I'm employed to flog, so I flog.” The guard Franz, who had been fairly restrained until now, perhaps expecting K.'s intervention to succeed, now came to the door wearing only his trousers, knelt down, clung to K.'s arm and whispered: “If you can't get mercy for both of us, at least try to free me. Willem is older than I am and less sensitive in every way. He also received a light flogging once, a few years ago, but I haven't yet been disgraced, and it was only Willem who led me into behaving as I did; he's my teacher in good and bad alike. My poor fiancée is waiting down in front of the bank to see how it turns out. I'm so miserably ashamed.” He dried his tear-soaked face on K.'s jacket. “I'm not waiting any longer,” said the flogger, gripping the rod in both hands and striking Franz while Willem crouched in a corner and watched secretly, not daring to turn his head. Then Franz's scream rose, unbroken and unchanging. It seemed to come not from a human being but from a tortured instrument; the whole corridor groaned with it, the entire building must hear it. “Don't scream!” K. cried, unable to restrain himself, and while looking tensely in the direction from which the attendants would have to come, he pushed Franz, not hard but hard enough for the man, beside himself, to fall and grope convulsively over the floor with his hands. Yet he did not escape the blows; the rod found him on the ground too, and as he writhed beneath it, its tip swung regularly up and down. Already an attendant appeared in the distance, with a second a few paces behind him. K. quickly slammed the door, went to a nearby window overlooking the courtyard, and opened it. The screaming had stopped completely. To keep the attendants from approaching, he called: “It's me.” “Good evening, Mr Authorised Signatory,” came the reply. “Has something happened?” “No, no,” K. answered. “It's only a dog howling in the courtyard.” When the attendants still did not move, he added: “You can carry on with your work.” To avoid being drawn into a conversation with them, he leaned out of the window. When after a little while he looked back into the corridor, they had gone. K., however, remained at the window; he did not dare go into the lumber room, nor did he want to go home. He was looking down into a small square courtyard, surrounded by offices. All the windows were now dark; only the uppermost caught a reflection of the moon. K. strained his eyes to penetrate the darkness of a corner where several handcarts had been pushed together. It tormented him that he had not succeeded in preventing the flogging, but the failure was not his fault. If Franz had not screamed—certainly it must have hurt terribly, but at a decisive moment one has to control oneself—if he had not screamed, K. would, at least very probably, have found another way to persuade the flogger. If the entire lowest rank of officials was a rabble, why should the flogger, who held the most inhuman office, be an exception? K. had clearly observed how his eyes shone at the sight of the banknote; he had evidently made the flogging serious only to raise the bribe a little further. And K. would not have stinted. He really was concerned to free the guards; now that he had begun fighting the corruption of this judicial system, it went without saying that he would intervene on this side too. But the moment Franz began screaming, everything was naturally over. K. could not allow the attendants, and perhaps all sorts of other people, to come and surprise him negotiating with the company in the lumber room. No one could really demand such a sacrifice from K. If he had intended to make it, it would almost have been simpler to undress himself and offer himself to the flogger in the guards' place. Besides, the flogger would certainly not have accepted this substitution, since without gaining any advantage he would nevertheless have gravely violated his duty, probably doubly so, for as long as K. was subject to proceedings he must surely be inviolable to all court employees. Admittedly, special regulations might apply here too. In any case, K. had been able to do nothing but slam the door, although even now that by no means removed every danger to him. That he had finally given Franz a push as well was regrettable, excusable only by his agitation.

In the distance he heard the attendants' footsteps. To avoid attracting their attention, he closed the window and went towards the main staircase. At the lumber-room door he stopped for a little while and listened. All was quiet. The man might have flogged the guards to death; they had been entirely in his power. K. had already reached for the handle, but withdrew his hand again. He could no longer help anyone, and the attendants were bound to arrive at any moment; but he vowed to raise the matter again and, as far as lay within his power, duly punish those truly guilty, the senior officials, not one of whom had yet dared to show himself to him. As he went down the bank's outside steps, he carefully observed everyone passing, but even farther away there was no girl to be seen waiting for anyone. Franz's remark that his fiancée was waiting proved to have been a lie, though a forgivable one, whose sole purpose had been to arouse greater pity.

Even the next day K. could not get the guards out of his mind. He was distracted at work, and to finish it had to stay in the office a little longer still than the day before. When, on his way home, he again passed the lumber room, he opened it out of habit. He could not collect himself at what he saw instead of the darkness he expected. Everything was unchanged, just as he had found it when opening the door the previous evening: the printed forms and ink bottles immediately beyond the threshold, the flogger with the rod, the guards still fully dressed, the candle on the shelf. And the guards began lamenting and cried: “Sir!” K. slammed the door at once and even beat his fists against it, as though that would close it more firmly. Almost weeping, he ran to the attendants, who were working quietly at the copying machines and stopped in surprise. “Clear out the lumber room at last!” he shouted. “We're sinking in filth.” The attendants were willing to do it the following day. K. nodded; now, late in the evening, he could no longer force them to work as he had actually intended. He sat down for a little while to keep the attendants nearby, shuffled some copies out of order, believing that this gave the impression he was checking them, and then, realising that the attendants would not dare leave at the same time as he did, went home tired and without a thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: One afternoon—K. was very busy just before the post went out—his uncle Karl, a small landowner from the country, pushed his way into the room between two attendants carrying in documents. The sight startled K. less than the thought of his uncle's coming had startled him some time before. His uncle was bound to come; K. had known that for about a month. Even then he had seemed to see him, slightly bent forward, his dented Panama hat in his left hand, extending his right towards him from a distance and thrusting it across the desk in reckless haste, knocking over everything in its path. His uncle was always in a hurry, haunted by the unfortunate idea that during his visits to the capital, which never lasted more than a day, he must manage everything he had planned and must also miss no conversation, business opportunity or pleasure that happened to present itself. K., who was particularly indebted to him as his former guardian, had to help him in every possible way and put him up for the night as well. He used to call him “the spectre from the country.”

Immediately after greeting him—he had no time to sit in the armchair K. offered—his uncle asked for a brief conversation in private. “It's necessary,” he said, swallowing with difficulty. “It's necessary for my peace of mind.” K. immediately sent the attendants out with instructions to admit no one. “What have I been hearing, Josef?” his uncle exclaimed when they were alone, sitting on the table and, without looking, stuffing various papers beneath himself to make his seat more comfortable. K. remained silent. He knew what was coming, but suddenly released from his strenuous work, he first gave himself over to a pleasant weariness and looked through the window at the opposite side of the street, of which only a small triangular section was visible from his seat, a piece of blank wall between two shop windows. “You're looking out of the window!” his uncle cried, throwing up his arms. “For heaven's sake, Josef, answer me. Is it true? Can it be true?” “Dear Uncle,” said K., wrenching himself out of his distraction, “I don't even know what you want from me.” “Josef,” his uncle said warningly, “you've always told the truth, as far as I know. Am I to take your last words as a bad sign?” “I can guess what you want,” K. said obediently. “You've probably heard about my case.” “That's right,” his uncle replied, nodding slowly. “I've heard about your case.” “From whom?” K. asked. “Erna wrote to me about it,” said his uncle. “She has no contact with you—you don't take much interest in her, unfortunately—but she found out all the same. I got the letter today and of course came straight here. For no other reason, but it seems reason enough. I can read you the passage about you.” He took the letter from his wallet. “Here it is. She writes: ‘I haven't seen Josef for a long time. Last week I went to the bank once, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't admitted. I waited nearly an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak to him; perhaps there'll be an opportunity soon. He sent me a large box of chocolates for my name day. It was very kind and thoughtful. I forgot to write and tell you at the time; only now that you ask do I remember. You must understand that chocolates disappear immediately at the boarding school. Scarcely have you realised that someone has given you chocolates when they're already gone. But about Josef, there was something else I wanted to tell you. As I mentioned, they wouldn't let me see him at the bank because he was in discussion with a gentleman. After waiting quietly for a while, I asked an attendant whether the discussion would last much longer. He said it probably would, because it was most likely about the case being brought against the authorised signatory. I asked what sort of case it was and whether he was mistaken, but he said he was not mistaken; it was a case, and a serious one, though he knew nothing more. He would gladly help the authorised signatory himself, since he was a good and fair gentleman, but he didn't know how to set about it and could only hope that influential gentlemen would take him under their protection. That was sure to happen, and everything would turn out well in the end, but for the present, judging by the authorised signatory's mood, things weren't going at all well. Naturally I attached little importance to this talk, tried to reassure the simple-minded attendant, forbade him to speak of it to others, and consider the whole thing gossip. Still, perhaps it would be good, dearest Father, if you looked into the matter on your next visit. It would be easy for you to find out more precisely what is happening and, if it really should be necessary, intervene through your important and influential acquaintances.
