I know of no case where it can be said with certainty that they intervened. They do defend some people, but one cannot bring it about by one's own will, they defend only those they wish to defend. The case they take on must, however, presumably have passed beyond the lower court already. In any event it is better not to think about them, for otherwise discussions with the other lawyers, their advice and their assistance, seem so repellent and useless, I've experienced it myself, that one would most like to throw everything aside, lie down in bed at home and hear no more about anything. But of course that would be the stupidest thing of all, and one would not have any peace in bed for long either.” “So you didn't think of the great lawyers then?” K. asked. “Not for long,” the merchant said, smiling again, “unfortunately one cannot forget them completely, night is particularly favourable to such thoughts. But at that time I wanted immediate results, so I went to the backstreet lawyers.”

“Look at the two of you sitting together!” cried Leni, who had returned with the tray and stopped in the doorway. They really were sitting close together, at the slightest turn their heads were bound to knock; the merchant, who besides being small also kept his back bent, had forced K. to stoop low as well if he wanted to hear everything. “Just a little longer,” K. called to Leni to keep her off, twitching impatiently the hand that he still had resting on the merchant's. “He wanted me to tell him about my trial,” the merchant said to Leni. “Go on telling him, go on,” she said. She spoke to the merchant affectionately, yet also condescendingly. K. did not like that; as he had now realised, the man did have a certain worth; for a start he had experience that he knew how to pass on well. Leni probably misjudged him. He watched with annoyance as Leni now took away the candle the merchant had been holding all this time, wiped his hand with her apron, then knelt beside him to scrape off some wax that had dripped from the candle onto his trousers. “You were going to tell me about the backstreet lawyers,” K. said, pushing Leni's hand away without further comment. “What do you want?” Leni asked, taking a light swipe at K. and continuing her work. “Yes, about the backstreet lawyers,” the merchant said, passing his hand over his forehead as if thinking. K. wanted to help him along and said: “You wanted immediate results and so you went to the backstreet lawyers.” “Quite right,” the merchant said, but did not continue. “Perhaps he doesn't want to speak of it in front of Leni,” K. thought, mastered his impatience to hear the rest there and then, and pressed him no further.

“Have you announced me?” he asked Leni. “Of course,” she said, “he's waiting for you. Leave Block now, you can talk to Block later too, he's staying here.” K. still hesitated. “You're staying here?” he asked the merchant; he wanted his own answer, he did not want Leni to speak of the merchant as though he were absent; today he was full of a secret anger towards Leni. And again it was only Leni who answered: “He often sleeps here.” “Sleeps here?” K. cried; he had thought the merchant would merely wait here for him while he swiftly finished his conversation with the lawyer, and then they would leave together and discuss everything thoroughly and undisturbed. “Yes,” Leni said, “not everyone is admitted to the lawyer at any hour they please, as you are, Josef. You don't seem at all surprised that, despite his illness, the lawyer receives you at eleven o'clock at night. You take what your friends do for you far too much for granted. Well, your friends, or I at least, do it gladly. I want no other thanks, and need no other, than for you to love me.” “Love you?” K. thought at first, and only then did it pass through his mind: “Well, yes, I do love her.” Nevertheless he said, disregarding everything else: “He receives me because I'm his client. If one needed outside help even for that, one would have to beg and give thanks at the same time with every step.” “How difficult he is today, isn't he?” Leni asked the merchant. “Now I'm the absent one,” K. thought, and almost even became angry with the merchant when, taking up Leni's rudeness, he said: “The lawyer receives him for other reasons as well. His case is more interesting than mine, you see. Besides, his trial is in its early stages, so probably not too muddled yet, and the lawyer still enjoys attending to it. Later it will be different.” “Yes, yes,” Leni said, looking at the merchant with a laugh, “how he chatters! You mustn't believe a word he says,” here she turned to K. “He's as talkative as he is sweet. Perhaps that's why the lawyer can't bear him either. In any case he only receives him when he's in the mood. I've gone to a great deal of trouble to change that, but it's impossible. Just think, sometimes I announce Block, but he doesn't receive him until the third day afterwards. And if Block isn't on the spot when he's called in, all is lost and he has to be announced afresh. That's why I've allowed Block to sleep here; it has happened that he's rung for him in the night. So now Block is ready at night too. Admittedly, what happens now is that when it turns out Block is here, the lawyer sometimes withdraws his order to admit him.” K. looked questioningly at the merchant. He nodded and said, as openly as he had spoken to K. earlier, perhaps distracted by shame: “Yes, later one becomes very dependent on one's lawyer.” “He only pretends to complain,” Leni said. “He very much likes sleeping here, as he has often admitted to me.” She went to a small door and pushed it open. “Do you want to see his bedroom?” she asked. K. went over and looked from the threshold into the low, windowless room, which was entirely filled by a narrow bed. To get into this bed one had to climb over its end. At the head of the bed was a recess in the wall, where a candle, an inkwell and a pen, as well as a bundle of papers, probably documents relating to the trial, stood in meticulous order. “You sleep in the maid's room?” K. asked, turning back to the merchant. “Leni has let me have it,” the merchant answered, “it's very advantageous.” K. looked at him for a long time; perhaps his first impression of the merchant had been right after all; he had experience, for his trial had been going on a long time, but he had paid dearly for that experience. Suddenly K. could no longer bear the sight of the merchant. “Put him to bed, then,” he called to Leni, who seemed not to understand him at all. He himself, however, wanted to go to the lawyer and, by dismissing him, free himself not only from the lawyer but also from Leni and the merchant. But before he had reached the door, the merchant addressed him in a quiet voice: “Mr Authorised Signatory.” K. turned round with an angry face. “You have forgotten your promise,” the merchant said, stretching pleadingly towards K. from his seat. “You were going to tell me a secret too.” “So I was,” K. said, his glance brushing Leni too, who was watching him attentively, “well then, listen: though it's almost no longer a secret. I'm going to the lawyer now to dismiss him.” “He's dismissing him,” the merchant cried, jumping from his chair and running round the kitchen with his arms raised. Again and again he cried: “He's dismissing the lawyer.” Leni was about to rush straight at K., but the merchant got in her way, for which she gave him a blow with her fists. Then, her hands still clenched into fists, she ran after K., who had a considerable head start. He had already entered the lawyer's room when Leni caught up with him. He had firmly closed the door behind him, but Leni, holding the door open with her foot, seized his arm and tried to pull him back. But he squeezed her wrist so hard that she had to let go of him with a sigh. She did not immediately dare to enter the room, and K. locked the door with the key.

“I've been waiting for you a very long time,” the lawyer said from the bed, laying a document he had been reading by the light of a candle on the bedside table and putting on a pair of spectacles through which he looked sharply at K. Instead of apologising K. said: “I'll be leaving again soon.” The lawyer had ignored K.'s remark, since it was not an apology, and said: “Next time I shall no longer admit you at this late hour.” “That fits in with the purpose of my visit,” K. said. The lawyer looked at him questioningly. “Sit down,” he said. “Since you wish it,” K. said, drawing a chair to the bedside table and sitting down. “It seemed to me you locked the door,” the lawyer said. “Yes,” K. said, “because of Leni.” He had no intention of sparing anyone. But the lawyer asked: “Was she being importunate again?” “Importunate?” K. asked. “Yes,” the lawyer said, laughing as he did so, having a fit of coughing and, once it had passed, beginning to laugh again. “Surely you've noticed her importunacy already,” he asked, patting the hand K. had absent-mindedly rested on the bedside table and now quickly withdrew. “You don't attach much importance to it,” the lawyer said when K. remained silent, “so much the better. Otherwise I might have had to apologise to you. It is a peculiarity of Leni's, which, incidentally, I forgave her long ago, and which I would not even mention if you had not just locked the door. This peculiarity, which I should probably least of all need to explain to you, but you are looking at me in such dismay that I shall do so, this peculiarity consists in Leni finding most accused men handsome. She attaches herself to all of them, loves all of them, and does indeed seem to be loved by all of them too; to entertain me she sometimes tells me about it afterwards, if I allow her. I am not as astonished by it all as you appear to be. If one has the right eye for it, one does often find accused men handsome. That is, admittedly, a curious phenomenon, one might almost say a phenomenon of natural science. Naturally there is no distinct, precisely ascertainable change in appearance as a result of the charge. It is not like other court cases, after all; most people retain their ordinary way of life and, if they have a good lawyer to look after them, are not greatly hindered by the trial. Nevertheless, those who have experience of it are able to pick out the accused men, one by one, from the largest crowd. By what? you will ask. My answer will not satisfy you. The accused men are simply the most handsome. It cannot be guilt that makes them handsome, for—at least I as a lawyer must speak in this way—not all of them are guilty; nor can it be the appropriate punishment that makes them handsome already, for not all of them are punished; so it can only lie in the proceedings brought against them, which somehow adhere to them. Admittedly, among the handsome there are some who are particularly handsome. But they are all handsome, even Block, that wretched worm.”

When the lawyer had finished, K. was entirely composed; he had even nodded conspicuously at the final words, thus confirming to himself his longstanding view that the lawyer always, and this time too, sought to distract him with general information unrelated to the matter and divert him from the main question of what actual work he had done on K.'s behalf. The lawyer presumably noticed that K. was offering him more resistance this time than usual, for he now fell silent to give K. the opportunity to speak himself, and then, as K. remained silent, asked: “Have you come to me today with a particular purpose?” “Yes,” K. said, shielding the candle a little with his hand so as to see the lawyer better, “I wanted to tell you that, as of today, I am ending your representation of me.” “Do I understand you correctly?” the lawyer asked, half rising in bed and supporting himself with one hand on the pillows. “I assume so,” K. said, sitting rigidly upright as though lying in wait. “Well, we can discuss this plan too,” the lawyer said after a little while. “It's no longer a plan,” K. said. “That may be,” the lawyer said, “but let us not rush anything all the same.” He used the word “us” as though he had no intention of releasing K., and as though, if he could no longer represent him, he wanted at least to remain his adviser. “It isn't rushed,” K. said, slowly rising and stepping behind his chair, “it has been carefully considered, perhaps even for too long. The decision is final.” “Then allow me just a few more words,” the lawyer said, lifting away the feather quilt and sitting on the edge of the bed. His bare, white-haired legs trembled with cold. He asked K. to pass him a blanket from the sofa. K. fetched the blanket and said: “You're risking a chill quite unnecessarily.” “The occasion is important enough,” the lawyer said, wrapping the feather quilt round his upper body and then winding the blanket round his legs. “Your uncle is my friend, and over time I have grown fond of you as well. I freely admit it. I need not be ashamed of it.” These sentimental speeches from the old man were very unwelcome to K., for they forced him into a fuller explanation that he would gladly have avoided, and, as he frankly admitted to himself, they unsettled him too, though they could never, of course, reverse his decision. “I thank you for your kindly feelings,” he said, “and I acknowledge that you have attended to my case as much as you are able, and as much as seems to you to be to my advantage. Recently, however, I have become convinced that this is not enough. Naturally I shall never attempt to persuade you, a man so much older and more experienced, to share my view; if at times I have involuntarily tried to do so, forgive me, but the matter is, as you yourself put it, important enough, and in my conviction it is necessary to intervene in the trial much more forcefully than has been done so far.” “I understand you,” the lawyer said, “you are impatient.” “I'm not impatient,” K. said, a little irritated and no longer watching his words so closely. “You must have noticed on my first visit, when I came to you with my uncle, that I cared little about the trial; unless I was reminded of it more or less forcibly, I forgot it altogether. But my uncle insisted that I entrust you with representing me, and I did so to please him. And surely one ought then to have expected the trial to weigh even less heavily on me than before, for one entrusts one's representation to a lawyer to shift a little of the burden of the trial off oneself. But the opposite happened. Never before had I had such great worries about the trial as I have had since you began representing me. When I was alone I did nothing about my case, but scarcely felt it; now, on the other hand, I had a representative, everything was in place for something to happen, unceasingly and with ever greater tension I awaited your intervention, but it did not come. You did, admittedly, give me various pieces of information about the court that I might not have been able to get from anyone else. But that cannot satisfy me when the trial is now, as it were, secretly pressing closer and closer to my body.” K. had pushed the chair away from him and stood erect, his hands in his jacket pockets. “After a certain point in one's practice,” the lawyer said quietly and calmly, “nothing essentially new ever happens. How many clients have stood before me as you do, at similar stages of their trials, and spoken in similar terms.” “Then,” K. said, “all those similar clients were just as right as I am. That does not refute me at all.” “I did not intend to refute you by it,” the lawyer said, “but I did want to add that I had expected more judgement from you than from others, particularly since I have given you more insight into the workings of the court and into my activities than I usually give clients. And now I must see that, despite everything, you do not have sufficient confidence in me. You do not make it easy for me.” How the lawyer abased himself before K.! Without any regard for the honour of his profession, which was surely most sensitive on precisely this point. And why was he doing it? To all appearances he was a very busy lawyer and moreover a rich man; in themselves neither the loss of earnings nor the loss of a client could matter much to him. Besides, he was sickly and should himself have been concerned to have work taken off his hands. And yet he held on to K. so tightly! Why? Was it personal affection for his uncle, or did he really consider K.'s trial so extraordinary and hope to distinguish himself in it, either for K. or—this possibility could simply never be excluded—for his friends at the court? Nothing could be read in the man himself, however ruthlessly K. scrutinised him. One might almost have supposed he was waiting with a deliberately closed expression to see the effect of his words. But he was evidently interpreting K.'s silence too favourably to himself when he now continued: “You will have noticed that although I have a large office, I employ no assistants. It used to be otherwise; there was a time when several young lawyers worked for me, today I work alone. This is connected partly with the change in my practice, as I confined myself more and more to legal cases of the same kind as yours, partly with the ever deeper understanding I acquired of these legal cases. I found that I could not leave this work to anyone else without sinning against my clients and the task I had undertaken. But the decision to do all the work myself had its natural consequences: I had to refuse almost all requests for representation and could give in only to those that touched me particularly closely—well, there are enough creatures, even quite nearby, who pounce on every scrap I throw away. And besides, I became ill from overwork. But all the same I do not regret my decision; it is possible that I should have refused more requests for representation than I did, but giving myself entirely to the trials I took on has proved absolutely necessary and has been rewarded by success. I once found, in a written work, a very fine expression of the difference between representation in ordinary legal cases and representation in these legal cases. It said: one lawyer leads his client by a thread as far as the judgement, but the other lifts his client straight onto his shoulders and carries him, without setting him down, to the judgement and beyond it. That is how it is. But it was not quite correct when I said I never regret this great labour. When, as in your case, it is so completely misunderstood, then, well then I almost regret it.” These speeches made K. more impatient than convinced. Somehow he thought he could hear in the lawyer's tone what awaited him if he gave in: the reassurances would begin again, the references to the progress of the petition, to the improved mood of the court officials, but also to the great difficulties obstructing the work—in short, everything familiar to the point of weariness would be brought out to deceive K. again with vague hopes and torment him with vague threats. That had to be prevented once and for all, so he said: “What do you intend to do in my case if you continue to represent me?” The lawyer submitted even to this insulting question and answered: “Carry on with what I have already undertaken for you.” “I knew it,” K. said, “but now any further word is superfluous.” “I shall make one more attempt,” the lawyer said, as though what was agitating K. were happening not to K. but to him. “You see, I suspect that you are led not only into a mistaken judgement of my legal assistance, but also into your other behaviour, by being treated too well despite being accused, or, more accurately, by being treated laxly, apparently laxly. This latter treatment has its reason too; it is often better to be in chains than free. But I should nevertheless like to show you how other accused men are treated; perhaps you will manage to learn a lesson from it. I am going to call Block in now; unlock the door and sit here beside the bedside table.” “Gladly,” K. said, doing what the lawyer had requested; he was always ready to learn. But to safeguard himself against any eventuality, he asked once more: “But you have taken note that I am ending your representation of me?” “Yes,” the lawyer said, “but you can still reverse it today.” He lay back down in bed, drew the feather quilt up to his knees and turned towards the wall. Then he rang.

Almost at the same moment as the bell rang, Leni appeared, trying with quick glances to discover what had happened; the fact that K. was sitting quietly beside the lawyer's bed seemed to reassure her. Smiling, she nodded to K., who stared at her. “Fetch Block,” the lawyer said. Instead of fetching him, though, she merely stepped outside the door, called: “Block! To the lawyer!” and then slipped behind K.'s chair, probably because the lawyer remained turned towards the wall and paid no attention to anything. From then on she disturbed him by leaning forwards over the back of the chair, or running her hands, very gently and carefully, to be sure, through his hair and stroking his cheeks. At last K. tried to stop her by taking hold of one of her hands, which, after some resistance, she surrendered to him.

Block had come at once when called, but stopped outside the door and seemed to be considering whether to enter. He raised his eyebrows and bent his head, as though listening for the command to come to the lawyer to be repeated. K. could have encouraged him to come in, but he had resolved to break definitively not only with the lawyer but with everything in this flat, and therefore remained motionless. Leni too was silent. Block noticed that at least no one was driving him away, and came in on tiptoe, his face tense, his hands clenched behind his back. He had left the door open for a possible retreat. He did not look at K. at all, but only ever at the high feather quilt, beneath which the lawyer, having moved right up close to the wall, was not even visible. But then his voice could be heard: “Block here?” he asked. This question struck Block, who had already moved a considerable distance forwards, almost like a blow to the chest and then one to the back; he staggered, stood still, deeply bent, and said: “At your service.” “What do you want?” the lawyer asked, “you've come at an inconvenient time.” “Wasn't I called?” Block asked, more of himself than of the lawyer, holding his hands out protectively and ready to run away. “You were called,” the lawyer said, “nevertheless you've come at an inconvenient time.” And after a pause he added: “You always come at an inconvenient time.” Since the lawyer had begun speaking, Block was no longer looking towards the bed; instead he stared somewhere into a corner and merely listened, as though the speaker's sidelong glance were too dazzling for him to bear. But listening was difficult too, for the lawyer spoke towards the wall, quietly and quickly. “Do you wish me to leave?” Block asked. “Now that you're here,” the lawyer said, “stay!” One might have thought the lawyer had not granted Block's wish but threatened him with a beating, for now Block really did begin to tremble. “Yesterday,” the lawyer said, “I was with the third judge, my friend, and gradually steered the conversation towards you. Do you want to know what he said?” “Oh, please,” Block said. As the lawyer did not answer at once, Block repeated his plea and bent down as though to kneel. But then K. snapped at him: “What are you doing?” he cried. As Leni had tried to stop him crying out, he seized her other hand too. It was not with the pressure of love that he held her fast; she also sighed repeatedly and tried to free her hands from his. But it was Block who was punished for K.'s cry, for the lawyer asked him: “Who is your lawyer?” “You are,” Block said. “And besides me?” the lawyer asked. “No one besides you,” Block said. “Then obey no one else either,” the lawyer said. Block fully acknowledged this; he measured K. with angry looks and shook his head vehemently at him. Had this behaviour been translated into words, it would have amounted to coarse abuse. And this was the man with whom K. had wanted to talk amicably about his own case! “I won't disturb you again,” K. said, leaning back in his chair. “Kneel down or crawl on all fours, do whatever you like, I won't concern myself with it.” But Block did have a sense of honour, towards K. at least, for he went up to him brandishing his fists and cried, as loudly as he dared in the lawyer's presence: “You mustn't speak to me like that, it isn't allowed. Why do you insult me? And here, what's more, in front of the lawyer, where both of us, you and I, are tolerated only out of charity? You are no better a man than I am, for you too are accused and have a trial. But if, despite that, you are still a gentleman, then I am just as much a gentleman, if not an even greater one. And I want to be addressed as such, particularly by you. But if you consider yourself privileged because you may sit here and listen quietly while I, as you put it, crawl on all fours, then I remind you of the old legal saying: for the suspect, movement is better than rest, for the man who rests may at any time, without knowing it, be on a pan of the scales and being weighed together with his sins.” K. said nothing, merely staring with unmoving eyes at this confused man. What changes had come over him in the last hour alone! Was it the trial that tossed him to and fro like this and prevented him from knowing where friend and where enemy stood? Did he not see that the lawyer was deliberately humiliating him and this time had no other purpose than to parade his power before K., and thereby perhaps bring K. into subjection too? But if Block was incapable of recognising this, or if he feared the lawyer so much that such recognition could not help him, how was it that he was nevertheless so clever or so bold as to deceive the lawyer and conceal from him that he had other lawyers working for him besides? And how did he dare to attack K., when K. could immediately betray his secret? But he dared still more: he went to the lawyer's bed and now began complaining about K. there as well: “Sir,” he said, “did you hear how this man spoke to me? One can still count the hours of his trial, and already he wants to offer sound advice to me, a man who has been on trial for five years. He even abuses me. Knows nothing and abuses me, who have studied precisely, as far as my feeble powers allow, what propriety, duty and the usages of the court demand.” “Pay no attention to anyone,” the lawyer said, “and do what seems right to you.” “Certainly,” Block said, as though encouraging himself, and with a brief sidelong glance now knelt right beside the bed. “I am kneeling now, my lawyer,” he said. But the lawyer remained silent. With one hand Block cautiously stroked the feather quilt. In the silence that now prevailed, Leni freed herself from K.'s hands and said: “You're hurting me. Let me go. I'm going to Block.” She went over and sat on the edge of the bed. Block was very pleased at her coming; with animated but silent gestures he immediately asked her to intercede with the lawyer for him. He evidently needed the lawyer's information very urgently, but perhaps only so that he could have his other lawyers make use of it. Leni probably knew exactly how to get at the lawyer; she pointed to his hand and pursed her lips as if for a kiss. Block immediately kissed the hand, and at a prompting from Leni repeated it twice more. But the lawyer still remained silent. Then Leni bent over the lawyer, the beautiful proportions of her body becoming visible as she stretched out like this, and, bending low towards his face, stroked his long white hair. This did at last extract an answer from him. “I hesitate to tell him,” the lawyer said, and one could see him shaking his head a little, perhaps to enjoy more of the pressure of Leni's hand. Block listened with his head lowered, as though by listening he were transgressing a commandment. “Why do you hesitate?” Leni asked. K. felt as though he were hearing a rehearsed conversation that had already been repeated many times, would be repeated many times more, and could never lose its novelty for Block alone. “How has he behaved today?” the lawyer asked instead of answering. Before Leni spoke on the subject she looked down at Block and watched for a little while as he raised his hands towards her and rubbed them together pleadingly. At last she nodded gravely, turned to the lawyer and said: “He was quiet and diligent.” An old merchant, a man with a long beard, was imploring a young girl for a favourable report. Even if he had ulterior motives in doing so, nothing could justify him in the eyes of a fellow human being. He almost degraded the spectator. So this was the effect of the lawyer's method, to which K. had fortunately not been exposed long enough: in the end the client forgot the whole world and hoped only to drag himself along this mistaken path to the end of the trial. This was no longer a client, this was the lawyer's dog. Had the lawyer ordered him to crawl under the bed as though into a kennel and bark from there, he would have done so with relish. As if commissioned to absorb precisely everything said here, report it to a higher authority and give an account, K. listened critically and with a sense of superiority. “What did he do throughout the day?” the lawyer asked. “I locked him,” Leni said, “in the maid's room, where he usually stays, so that he wouldn't disturb me in my work. Through the opening I could look in from time to time to see what he was doing. He was always kneeling on the bed, with the writings you lent him open on the windowsill, reading them. That made a good impression on me; the window only opens onto an air shaft, you see, and gives almost no light. The fact that Block read all the same showed me how obedient he is.” “I am pleased to hear that,” the lawyer said. “But did he read with understanding?” During this conversation Block moved his lips incessantly; evidently he was forming the answers he hoped to hear from Leni. “Of course I can't answer that with certainty,” Leni said. “In any case I saw that he read thoroughly. He spent the whole day reading the same page and ran his finger along the lines as he read. Every time I looked in at him, he sighed, as though the reading cost him a great effort. The writings you lent him are probably difficult to understand.” “Yes,” the lawyer said, “they certainly are. I don't believe he understands anything of them either. They are only meant to give him an idea of how difficult the struggle is that I wage in his defence. And for whom do I wage this difficult struggle? For—it is almost ridiculous to say it—for Block. He is to learn to grasp what that means as well. Did he study without interruption?” “Almost without interruption,” Leni answered, “only once did he ask me for some water to drink. Then I passed him a glass through the hatch. At eight o'clock I let him out and gave him something to eat.” Block glanced sideways at K., as though praiseworthy things were being said about him here which must impress K. too. He seemed hopeful now, moved more freely and shifted to and fro on his knees. All the more clearly could one see how he stiffened under the lawyer's next words. “You praise him,” the lawyer said. “But that is precisely what makes it hard for me to speak. You see, the judge did not speak favourably, either of Block himself or of his trial.” “Not favourably?” Leni asked. “How is that possible?” Block looked at her with such a tense gaze that he seemed to credit her with the power, even now, to turn the judge's long-since spoken words in his favour. “Not favourably,” the lawyer said. “He was even unpleasantly affected when I began to speak of Block. Don't speak of Block, he said. He is my client, I said. You are letting yourself be used, he said. I do not consider his case lost, I said. You are letting yourself be used, he repeated. I don't believe so, I said. Block is diligent in his trial and always pursuing his case. He practically lives with me so as to keep abreast of things at all times. One does not always find such zeal. Certainly, he is not personally agreeable, he has ugly manners and is dirty, but where the proceedings are concerned he is beyond reproach. I said beyond reproach, I deliberately exaggerated. At that he said: Block is merely cunning. He has accumulated a great deal of experience and knows how to drag out the trial. But his ignorance is much greater still than his cunning. What would he say if he learnt that his trial has not yet even begun, if he were told that the bell signalling the start of the trial has not even been rung yet. Be still, Block,” the lawyer said, for Block was just beginning to rise on unsteady knees and evidently wanted to ask for an explanation. This was now the first time the lawyer had addressed Block directly at any length. With tired eyes he looked half aimlessly, half down at Block, who beneath this gaze slowly sank back onto his knees. “That remark of the judge's has no significance for you at all,” the lawyer said. “Don't take fright at every word. If that happens again, I shan't tell you anything more. One cannot begin a sentence without your looking at one as though your final judgement were about to come. Have some shame in front of my client here! You also shake the confidence he places in me. What do you want? You are still alive, you are still under my protection. Senseless fear! You have read somewhere that in some cases the final judgement comes without warning, from any mouth at any time. With many qualifications that is indeed true, but it is equally true that your fear disgusts me and that I see in it a lack of the necessary confidence. What did I say, then? I repeated a remark by a judge. You know, the different views heap themselves around the proceedings until they become impenetrable. This judge, for example, places the start of the proceedings at a different point from the one I do. A difference of opinion, nothing more. At a certain stage of the trial, according to ancient custom, a bell is rung. In this judge's view, the trial begins with that. I cannot now tell you everything that speaks against it, nor would you understand it; let it be enough for you that much speaks against it.” Below, Block ran his fingers awkwardly through the fur of the bedside rug; his fear at the judge's pronouncement at times made him forget his own subservience towards the lawyer; then he thought only of himself and turned the judge's words over in every direction. “Block,” Leni said in a warning tone, pulling him up a little by the collar of his jacket. “Leave the fur alone now and listen to the lawyer.” K. could not understand how the lawyer could have thought to win him over by this display. Had he not driven him away already, he would have achieved it through this scene.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: K. was given the assignment of showing some of the city's artistic monuments to an Italian business associate of the bank, a man of great importance to it, who was visiting the city for the first time. At any other time he would certainly have regarded the assignment as an honour, but now, when he could maintain his standing in the bank only with great effort, he took it on reluctantly. Every hour he was kept away from the office worried him; admittedly he could no longer make anything like the use of his office hours that he once had, he spent many an hour preserving only the most makeshift appearance of actual work, but his worries were all the greater when he was not in the office. Then he thought he could see the deputy manager, who had always been lying in wait, coming into his office from time to time, sitting down at his desk, searching through his papers, receiving clients with whom K. had been almost on friendly terms for years and winning them away from him, perhaps even uncovering mistakes by which K., as he worked, now always felt threatened from a thousand directions and which he could no longer avoid. Whenever, therefore, he was assigned a business errand or even a short trip, however much of a distinction it might be presented as — such assignments had quite by chance become more frequent lately — the suspicion was nevertheless close at hand that they wanted to remove him from the office for a while and check his work, or at least that they considered him easy to do without in the office. He could have turned down most of these assignments without difficulty, but he did not dare, for if his fear had even the slightest foundation, refusing the assignment meant admitting his anxiety. For this reason he accepted such assignments with apparent indifference and even, when he was to make a tiring two-day business trip, kept quiet about a bad cold, simply to avoid the risk of being prevented from travelling on the grounds of the rainy autumn weather then prevailing. When he returned from this trip with a raging headache, he learned that he had been chosen to accompany the Italian business associate the following day. The temptation to refuse at least this once was very great, especially since what had been planned for him here was not work directly connected with business, but fulfilling this social obligation towards the business associate was in itself undoubtedly important enough, only not for K., who knew very well that he could hold his own only through success in his work, and that if he failed in this, it would be utterly worthless even if he should unexpectedly charm this Italian; he did not want to be pushed out of the sphere of work even for a single day, for the fear of not being allowed back in was too great, a fear he recognised perfectly well as exaggerated, but which still oppressed him. In this case, though, it was almost impossible to invent an acceptable objection, K.'s knowledge of Italian was certainly not very extensive, but it was sufficient; the decisive thing, however, was that K. possessed some knowledge of art from earlier times, a fact that had become known in the bank in a hugely exaggerated form because K. had for a time been a member of the society for the preservation of the city's artistic monuments, and that, incidentally, only for business reasons. Now the Italian, so rumour had it, was an art lover, and the choice of K. as his companion was therefore a matter of course.

It was a very rainy, stormy morning when K., full of resentment at the day ahead of him, arrived at the office as early as seven, so that he could at least finish some work before the visitor drew him away from everything. He was very tired, for he had spent half the night studying an Italian grammar to prepare himself a little, the window, where he had lately been in the habit of sitting far too often, attracted him more than the desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. Unfortunately the attendant came in just then and announced that the manager had sent him to see whether the authorised signatory was here yet; if he was, would he be so kind as to come over to the reception room, the gentleman from Italy was already there. “I'm coming,” said K., slipped a small dictionary into his pocket, tucked an album of the city's sights which he had prepared for the foreign visitor under his arm, and went through the deputy manager's office into the manager's office. He was glad to have come to the office so early and to be available at once, something no one could seriously have expected. The deputy manager's office was of course still empty, as though it were the middle of the night, the attendant had probably been meant to summon him to the reception room too, but had had no success. When K. entered the reception room the two gentlemen rose from their deep armchairs. The manager smiled in a friendly way, he was evidently very pleased that K. had come, he made the introductions at once, the Italian shook K.'s hand vigorously and laughingly called somebody an early riser, K. did not quite understand whom he meant, besides, it was an odd word whose meaning K. guessed only after a little while. He replied with a few fluent sentences which the Italian again received with laughter, several times passing a nervous hand over his bushy grey-blue moustache. This moustache was evidently perfumed, one almost felt tempted to go closer and smell it. Once they were all seated and a little preliminary conversation began, K. noticed to his great discomfort that he understood the Italian only in fragments. When he spoke quite calmly, K. understood him almost completely, but these were only rare exceptions, most of the time speech poured out of his mouth, he shook his head as though in delight at it. In such speeches, however, he regularly became entangled in some dialect which for K. no longer had anything Italian about it, but which the manager not only understood but spoke, something K. might certainly have foreseen, for the Italian came from southern Italy, where the manager too had spent several years. At all events K. realised that he had been deprived of most of his opportunity to communicate with the Italian, for his French too was difficult to understand, and the moustache concealed the movements of his lips, the sight of which might have helped with understanding. K. began to foresee a great deal of unpleasantness, for the time being he gave up trying to understand the Italian — in the presence of the manager, who understood him so easily, it would have been wasted effort — and confined himself to watching him resentfully, how he rested deep yet lightly in his armchair, how he repeatedly tugged at his short, sharply cut jacket, and how once, with raised arms and hands moving loosely at the wrists, he tried to depict something which K. could not grasp, although he leaned forward and never took his eyes off the hands. Finally K., who otherwise had nothing to do and was merely following the exchange of speeches mechanically with his eyes, began to feel his earlier fatigue, and once, to his horror, fortunately still in time, he caught himself just about to get up, turn round and walk away in his absent-mindedness. At last the Italian looked at his watch and sprang up. Having taken his leave of the manager, he pressed up against K., so close indeed that K. had to push his armchair back to be able to move. The manager, who must have recognised in K.'s eyes the distress this Italian was causing him, joined the conversation, so skilfully and so tactfully that he appeared merely to be adding little pieces of advice, whereas in fact he was very briefly making everything the Italian said comprehensible to K., while the Italian kept tirelessly interrupting him. From him K. learned that the Italian still had some business to attend to for the moment, that unfortunately he would have little time altogether, that he certainly did not intend to rush round all the sights either, that instead — though only if K. agreed, the decision rested with him alone — he had decided to visit only the cathedral, but to see it thoroughly. He was immensely pleased to be able to make this visit in the company of so learned and obliging a man — this meant K., whose sole occupation was to block out the Italian and quickly take in the manager's words — and he asked him, if the hour suited him, to be at the cathedral in two hours, at about ten. He himself hoped to be there without fail by that time. K. made a few appropriate replies, the Italian shook hands first with the manager, then with K., then once more with the manager, and, followed by them both, went towards the door, only half turned towards them now, but still without ceasing to talk. K. then remained a little while with the manager, who looked particularly unwell today. He seemed to think he owed K. some sort of apology and said — they were standing close together in confidence — that at first he had meant to go with the Italian himself, but then — he gave no further reason — he had decided that he would rather send K. If he did not understand the Italian immediately at the start, he must not let that disconcert him, understanding came very quickly, and even if there was much he did not understand at all, that was not so bad either, since being understood was not all that important to the Italian. Besides, K.'s Italian was surprisingly good and he would certainly handle the matter very well. With that K. was dismissed. He spent the time still left to him writing out of the dictionary unusual words that he would need to guide the visitor round the cathedral. It was an extremely tedious task, attendants brought the post, clerks came with various enquiries and, seeing K. occupied, remained standing at the door but would not move away until K. had heard them, the deputy manager did not miss the opportunity to disturb K., came in several times, took the dictionary out of his hand and leafed through it for no apparent purpose, even clients appeared in the half-darkness of the anteroom when the door opened and bowed hesitantly, they wanted to draw attention to themselves but were uncertain whether they were being seen — all this moved around K. as its centre, while he himself assembled the words he needed, then looked them up in the dictionary, then wrote them out, then practised their pronunciation and finally tried to learn them by heart. But his formerly good memory seemed to have deserted him altogether, sometimes he became so furious with the Italian who was causing him this exertion that he buried the dictionary under papers with the firm intention of doing no more preparation, but then he saw that he could hardly walk up and down in silence with the Italian in front of the works of art in the cathedral, and with even greater fury he brought the dictionary out again.

Just at half past nine, as he was about to leave, there was a telephone call, Leni wished him good morning and asked how he was, K. thanked her hurriedly and remarked that he could not possibly enter into a conversation now, as he had to go to the cathedral. “To the cathedral?” Leni asked. “Yes, to the cathedral.” “But why to the cathedral?” said Leni. K. tried to explain briefly, but he had scarcely begun when Leni suddenly said: “They're hounding you.” K. could not bear pity which he had neither invited nor expected, he said goodbye in two words, yet as he hung the receiver back in its place he said, half to himself, half to the distant girl who could no longer hear him: “Yes, they're hounding me.”

But now it was already late, there was almost a danger of his not arriving in time. He went by motor car, at the last moment he had remembered the album, which he had found no opportunity to hand over earlier and which he therefore took with him now. He held it on his knees and drummed restlessly on it throughout the journey. The rain had eased, but it was damp, cold and dark, there would be little to see in the cathedral, whereas K.'s cold would grow much worse there from standing for a long time on the cold tiles.

Cathedral Square was quite empty, K. remembered noticing even as a small child that almost all the window blinds in the houses of this narrow square were always lowered. In today's weather, admittedly, this was more understandable than usual. The cathedral seemed empty too, naturally it occurred to no one to come here now. K. went through both side aisles, he met only an old woman who, wrapped in a warm shawl, was kneeling before a picture of the Virgin and looking at it. In the distance he also saw a limping attendant disappear through a doorway in the wall. K. had arrived punctually, ten had struck just as he entered, but the Italian was not here yet. K. went back to the main entrance, stood there indecisively for a time, then walked round the cathedral in the rain to see whether the Italian might be waiting at some side entrance. He was nowhere to be found. Could the manager have misunderstood the time? How could anyone understand this man properly anyway. But however that might be, K. had in any case to wait half an hour for him to begin with. Since he was tired he wanted to sit down, he went back into the cathedral, found a small scrap of something like carpet on a step, dragged it with the toe of his shoe in front of a nearby pew, wrapped himself more tightly in his coat, turned up his collar and sat down. To distract himself he opened the album and leafed through it a little, but soon had to stop, for it was growing so dark that when he looked up he could scarcely distinguish a single detail in the nearby side aisle.

In the distance a large triangle of candle flames glittered on the high altar, K. could not have said with certainty whether he had seen them earlier. Perhaps they had only just been lit. Church attendants creep about by profession, one does not notice them. When K. happened to turn round, he saw a tall thick candle fastened to a pillar not far behind him burning too. Beautiful as this was, it was wholly insufficient to light the altar paintings, most of which hung in the darkness of the side altars, indeed it increased the darkness. It was as sensible as it was discourteous of the Italian not to have come, there would have been nothing to see, they would have had to content themselves with examining a few pictures inch by inch with K.'s electric torch. To test what might be expected of this, K. went to a nearby small side chapel, climbed a few steps to a low marble balustrade and, bending over it, shone his torch on the altarpiece. The sanctuary lamp hung in front of it, interfering with his view. The first thing K. saw, and partly guessed at, was a large knight in armour depicted at the very edge of the picture. He was leaning on his sword, which he had driven into the bare ground in front of him — only a few blades of grass sprang up here and there. He seemed to be watching attentively an event taking place before him. It was astonishing that he remained standing like that and did not go closer. Perhaps he had been appointed to stand guard. K., who had not seen any pictures for a long time, looked at the knight for quite a while, although he had to keep blinking, as he could not bear the green light of the torch. Then, when he swept the light over the rest of the picture, he found an entombment of Christ treated in the usual manner, it was, incidentally, a fairly recent picture. He put the torch in his pocket and returned to his seat.

It was probably pointless now to wait for the Italian, but outside it was certainly pouring with rain, and since it was not as cold here as K. had expected, he decided to stay for the time being. Near him was the great pulpit, on its small round canopy two empty golden crosses were set at an angle, almost lying down, crossing at their very tips. The outer wall of the parapet and its transition to the supporting pillar were formed of green foliage into which little angels reached, some lively, some at rest. K. stepped in front of the pulpit and examined it from every side, the stone had been worked with extraordinary care, the deep darkness between the leaves and behind them seemed caught and held fast, K. put his hand into one of these gaps and then carefully felt the stone, until now he had known nothing of this pulpit's existence. Then, by chance, he noticed a church attendant behind the next row of pews, standing there in a loose, creased black coat, holding a snuffbox in his left hand and looking at him. “What does the man want?” K. thought. “Does he find me suspicious? Does he want a tip?” But now, when the church attendant saw that K. had noticed him, he pointed with his right hand, still holding a pinch of snuff between two fingers, in some indefinite direction. His behaviour was almost incomprehensible, K. waited a little longer, but the church attendant kept pointing at something and reinforced it with nods of his head. “What does he want?” K. asked softly, he did not dare call out here; but then he took out his wallet and squeezed along the nearest pew to get to the man. The latter, however, immediately made a rejecting gesture with his hand, shrugged his shoulders and limped away. With a gait like this hurried limping, K. as a child had tried to imitate riding a horse. “A childish old man,” K. thought, “he has only enough sense left for church duties. How he stops when I stop, and how he watches to see whether I mean to go on.” Smiling, K. followed the old man through the whole side aisle almost as far as the high altar, the old man kept pointing at something, but K. deliberately did not turn round, the pointing served no purpose except to put him off the old man's trail. Finally he did leave him alone, he did not want to frighten him too much, nor did he want to scare the figure away altogether in case the Italian should still arrive.

As he stepped into the nave to find his seat, where he had left the album, he noticed on a pillar almost adjoining the choir stalls a small secondary pulpit, very plain, of bare, pale stone. It was so small that from a distance it looked like a niche still empty, intended to hold a statue. The preacher certainly could not take a full step back from the parapet. Moreover, the pulpit's stone vault began unusually low and, though rising without any ornament, curved upwards in such a way that a man of average height could not stand upright there, but had to remain bent over the parapet. The whole thing seemed intended to torment the preacher, it was impossible to understand why this pulpit was needed when the other one, so large and so elaborately decorated, was available.

K. would certainly not have noticed this small pulpit either if there had not been a lamp fixed at the top, of the kind usually put in readiness just before a sermon. Was a sermon about to take place? In the empty church? K. looked down the staircase which, hugging the pillar, led up to the pulpit and was so narrow that it seemed intended not for people but merely to ornament the pillar. But at the foot of the pulpit, K. smiled in astonishment, a priest really was standing, his hand on the banister, ready to climb up, and looking towards K. Then he gave a very slight nod, whereupon K. crossed himself and bowed, something he should have done earlier. The priest gave himself a little swing upwards and climbed the pulpit with short, quick steps. Was a sermon really about to begin? Perhaps the church attendant had not been quite out of his mind after all and had wanted to drive K. towards the preacher, which admittedly had been extremely necessary in the empty church. Besides, there was still an old woman somewhere before a picture of the Virgin who ought to have come too. And if there was to be a sermon, why was it not introduced by the organ? But the organ remained silent and merely gleamed faintly out of the darkness of its great height.

K. considered whether he should not leave as quickly as possible now; if he did not do so now, there was no prospect of being able to do so during the sermon, he would then have to stay as long as it lasted, he was losing so much time at the office, he had long since ceased to be obliged to wait for the Italian, he looked at his watch, it was eleven. But could a sermon really be preached? Could K. alone constitute the congregation? What if he had been a stranger who only wanted to look round the church? At bottom that was all he was. It was absurd to think that a sermon was to be preached, now at eleven, on a weekday, in the foulest weather. The priest — there was no doubt that he was a priest, a young man with a smooth, dark face — was evidently only going up to extinguish the lamp, which had been lit by mistake.

But that was not the case, instead the priest examined the light and turned it up a little further, then slowly turned towards the parapet and took hold of its angular front edge with both hands. He stood like that for a time, looking about without moving his head. K. had retreated some distance and was leaning with his elbows on the foremost pew. With uncertain eyes he saw the church attendant somewhere, without being able to determine the exact spot, crouching with a bent back, peacefully, as though his task were done. What silence now reigned in the cathedral! But K. had to disturb it, he had no intention of staying here; if it was the priest's duty to preach at a particular hour regardless of the circumstances, then let him do so, he would manage without K.'s assistance, just as K.'s presence would certainly not increase the effect. So K. slowly set off, felt his way on tiptoe along the pew, then reached the broad central aisle and walked quite undisturbed there too, except that the stone floor rang beneath the lightest step and the vaults echoed it faintly but continually, in a repeated progression governed by laws. K. felt a little abandoned as he walked alone between the empty pews, perhaps watched by the priest, the size of the cathedral too seemed to him to lie just at the limit of what human beings could still bear. When he reached his former seat, he positively snatched, without pausing further, at the album he had left lying there and took it with him. He had almost left the area of the pews and was approaching the open space between them and the exit when for the first time he heard the priest's voice. A powerful, trained voice. How it penetrated the cathedral, which stood ready to receive it! But it was not the congregation the priest was calling to, it was quite unambiguous and there could be no evasion, he called: Josef K.!

K. stopped short and looked at the floor in front of him. For the moment he was still free, he could still walk on and slip away through one of the three small dark wooden doors not far ahead of him. It would simply mean that he had not understood, or that although he had understood, he did not intend to concern himself with it. But if he turned round he was held fast, for then he had admitted that he had understood perfectly, that he really was the person being called and that he also intended to obey. Had the priest called again, K. would certainly have gone away, but since everything remained silent, however long K. waited, he did turn his head a little after all, for he wanted to see what the priest was doing now. He stood calmly in the pulpit as before, but it was quite clear that he had noticed K.'s turning his head. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. had not now turned round completely. He did so and the priest beckoned him closer with a finger. Since everything could now be done openly, he ran — he did so from curiosity too, and to shorten the affair — towards the pulpit with long, flying strides. He stopped at the first pews, but the distance still seemed too great to the priest, he stretched out his hand and pointed with a sharply lowered forefinger to a spot immediately in front of the pulpit. K. obeyed in this too, from this position he had to tilt his head far back to see the priest at all. “You are Josef K.,” said the priest, raising one hand from the parapet in an indefinite gesture. “Yes,” said K., he thought of how openly he had always given his name before, for some time now it had been a burden to him, and now people he was meeting for the first time knew his name as well; how pleasant it was to introduce oneself first and only then to be known. “You are accused,” said the priest, particularly quietly. “Yes,” said K., “I have been informed of that.” “Then you are the man I am looking for,” said the priest. “I am the prison chaplain.” “I see,” said K. “I had you summoned here,” said the priest, “to speak with you.” “I didn't know,” said K. “I came here to show an Italian round the cathedral.” “Leave aside what is incidental,” said the priest. “What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer book?” “No,” K. answered, “it's an album of the city's sights.” “Put it down,” said the priest. K. flung it away so violently that it fell open and slid some distance over the floor with its pages crumpled. “Do you know that your trial is going badly?” the priest asked. “It seems that way to me too,” said K. “I have made every effort, but so far without success. Though I haven't finished the submission yet.” “How do you imagine it will end?” the priest asked. “I used to think it must end well,” said K., “now I sometimes doubt that myself. I don't know how it will end. Do you know?” “No,” said the priest, “but I fear it will end badly. You are considered guilty. Your trial may never get beyond a lower court. For the time being at least, your guilt is considered proven.” “But I'm not guilty,” said K. “It's a mistake. How can a human being be guilty at all. We're all human beings here, each one of us like the next.” “That is true,” said the priest, “but that is how the guilty tend to speak.” “Are you prejudiced against me too?” K. asked. “I am not prejudiced against you,” said the priest. “Thank you,” said K. “But everyone else involved in the proceedings is prejudiced against me. They instil it into those who aren't involved as well. My position is becoming more and more difficult.” “You misunderstand the facts,” said the priest. “The judgement does not come all at once, the proceedings gradually pass over into the judgement.” “So that is how it is,” said K., lowering his head. “What do you intend to do next in your case?” the priest asked. “I intend to look for more help,” said K., raising his head to see how the priest judged this. “There are still certain possibilities I haven't made use of.” “You look too much for help from others,” said the priest disapprovingly, “and especially from women. Don't you see that it is not the true help.” “Sometimes, indeed often, I could agree with you,” said K., “but not always. Women have great power. If I could persuade a few women I know to work together for me, I would have to get through. Especially with this court, which consists almost entirely of womanisers. Show the examining magistrate a woman in the distance and he will charge over the court table and the accused just to get there in time.” The priest lowered his head towards the parapet, only now did the canopy of the pulpit seem to be pressing him down. What sort of storm could be raging outside? This was no longer a gloomy day, it was already the depths of night. None of the stained glass in the great windows could break the dark wall with so much as a glimmer. And just now the church attendant began putting out the candles on the high altar one after another. “Are you angry with me?” K. asked the priest. “Perhaps you don't know what sort of court you serve.” He received no answer. “It's only what I've experienced,” said K. Above him it was still silent. “I didn't mean to insult you,” said K. Then the priest shouted down at K.: “Can't you see two steps ahead?” It was shouted in anger, but at the same time like someone who sees another person falling and, himself startled, cries out unguardedly, against his will.

Now both remained silent for a long time. Certainly the priest could not make K. out clearly in the darkness below, whereas K. saw the priest distinctly in the light of the small lamp. Why did the priest not come down? He had not delivered a sermon, after all, but merely told K. a few things which, if he paid them close attention, would probably do him more harm than good. Yet the priest's good intentions seemed beyond doubt to K., it was not impossible that if he came down K. might reach an understanding with him, it was not impossible that he might get from him decisive and acceptable advice which would show him, for example, not how to influence the trial, but how to break out of the trial, how to get round it, how to live outside the trial. This possibility must exist, K. had thought of it quite often lately. But if the priest knew of such a possibility, perhaps he would reveal it if asked, even though he himself belonged to the court and even though, when K. had attacked the court, he had suppressed his gentle nature and even shouted at K.

“Won't you come down?” said K. “There's no sermon to give, after all. Come down to me.” “I can come now,” said the priest, perhaps he regretted his shouting. As he took the lamp off its hook, he said: “I had to speak with you from a distance first. Otherwise I let myself be influenced too easily and forget my duty.”

K. waited for him at the foot of the stairs. The priest held out his hand to him from one of the upper steps as he came down. “Have you a little time for me?” K. asked. “As much time as you need,” said the priest, handing K. the little lamp to carry. Even at close quarters a certain solemnity did not leave his manner. “You're very kind to me,” said K. They walked up and down together in the dark side aisle. “You're an exception among everyone who belongs to the court. I have more trust in you than in any of them, and I already know so many. I can speak openly with you.” “Do not deceive yourself,” said the priest. “What should I be deceiving myself about?” K. asked. “You deceive yourself about the court,” said the priest, “in the introductory writings to the Law it says of this deception: a gatekeeper stands before the Law. A man from the country comes to this gatekeeper and requests admission to the Law. But the gatekeeper says he cannot grant him admission at this moment. The man considers this and then asks whether he will be allowed to enter later, in that case. ‘Possibly,’ the gatekeeper says, ‘but not at the moment.’ As the gate to the Law stands open as it always does, and the gatekeeper moves aside, the man stoops to look inside through the gate. Seeing this, the gatekeeper laughs and says: ‘If it attracts you so, just try going in despite my prohibition. But bear this in mind: I am powerful. And I am only the lowest of the gatekeepers. There are gatekeepers stationed from one hall to the next, each more powerful than the last. Even I cannot bear the sight of so much as the third.’ The man from the country has not expected difficulties like these, surely the Law ought to be accessible to everyone at all times, he thinks, but as he now looks more closely at the gatekeeper in his fur coat, at his large pointed nose, his long, thin, black Tartar beard, he decides, after all, that he would rather wait until he is given permission to enter. The gatekeeper gives him a stool and allows him to sit down to one side of the door. There he sits for days and years. He makes many attempts to be admitted and wears the gatekeeper out with his requests. The gatekeeper often conducts little interrogations, questioning him about his homeland and many other things, but the questions are indifferent ones, of the sort great gentlemen ask, and at the end he always tells him again that he cannot let him in yet. The man, who has equipped himself with many things for his journey, uses everything, however valuable, to bribe the gatekeeper. The latter accepts everything, but as he does so he says: ‘I accept it only so that you won't think you've failed to try something.’ Throughout the many years the man watches the gatekeeper almost continuously. He forgets the other gatekeepers and this first one seems to him the only obstacle to admission to the Law. He curses the unfortunate chance, loudly in the early years, later, as he grows old, he only mutters to himself. He becomes childish, and since, in studying the gatekeeper for years, he has also come to recognise the fleas in his fur collar, he asks the fleas too to help him and change the gatekeeper's mind. Finally his eyesight weakens and he does not know whether it really is growing darker around him or whether his eyes are merely deceiving him. Yet in the darkness he now recognises a radiance that streams inextinguishably from the door of the Law. He has little time left to live now. Before his death, all the experiences of the entire time gather in his head into one question which he has not yet put to the gatekeeper. He beckons to him, as he can no longer straighten his stiffening body. The gatekeeper has to bend down low over him, for the difference in their heights has changed very much to the man's disadvantage. ‘What else do you want to know now?’ the gatekeeper asks, ‘you are insatiable.’ ‘Everyone strives towards the Law, after all,’ says the man, ‘how is it that in all these years no one except me has asked to be admitted.’ The gatekeeper recognises that the man is already at his end and, to reach his failing hearing, bellows at him: ‘No one else could be admitted here, because this entrance was intended for you alone. I am going now to close it.’”

“So the gatekeeper deceived the man,” said K. at once, powerfully drawn to the story. “Do not be hasty,” said the priest, “do not take over someone else's opinion without examining it. I have told you the story in the words of the text. It says nothing about deception.” “But it's clear,” said K., “and your first interpretation was quite right. The gatekeeper gave him the liberating information only when it could no longer help the man.” “He was not asked earlier,” said the priest, “consider too that he was only a gatekeeper, and as such he fulfilled his duty.” “Why do you believe he fulfilled his duty?” K. asked, “he didn't fulfil it. His duty may have been to turn away all strangers, but this man, for whom the entrance was intended, he should have let in.” “You have too little respect for the text and are altering the story,” said the priest. “The story contains two important statements by the gatekeeper about admission to the Law, one at the beginning, one at the end. One passage says: he cannot grant him admission at this moment, and the other: this entrance was intended for you alone. If there were a contradiction between these two statements, then you would be right and the gatekeeper would have deceived the man. But there is no contradiction. On the contrary, the first statement even points towards the second. One could almost say that the gatekeeper went beyond his duty by holding out to the man the prospect of a future possibility of admission. At that time his duty seems to have been merely to turn the man away, and indeed many commentators on the text wonder why the gatekeeper made that suggestion at all, for he seems to love precision and watches strictly over his office. For many years he does not leave his post and closes the gate only at the very end, he is very conscious of the importance of his service, for he says: ‘I am powerful,’ he respects his superiors, for he says: ‘I am only the lowest of the gatekeepers,’ he is not talkative, for throughout the many years he asks only what are called ‘indifferent’ questions, he cannot be bribed, for of a gift he says: ‘I accept it only so that you won't think you've failed to try something,’ where the fulfilment of duty is concerned he can be neither moved nor embittered, for it is said of the man that he ‘wears the gatekeeper out with his requests,’ finally his outward appearance too indicates a pedantic character, the large pointed nose and the long, thin, black Tartar beard. Could there be a more dutiful gatekeeper. But other traits are mixed into the gatekeeper's nature, traits very favourable to the person requesting admission, and which do after all make it understandable that, in suggesting that future possibility, he could go a little beyond his duty. For it cannot be denied that he is a little simple-minded and, in connection with this, a little conceited. Even if his remarks about his power and the power of the other gatekeepers and their appearance, unbearable even to him — I say, even if all these remarks may be correct in themselves, the way he makes them nevertheless shows that his understanding is clouded by simplicity and arrogance. The commentators say of this: ‘Understanding a thing correctly and misunderstanding the same thing do not entirely exclude one another.’ But in any case one must assume that this simplicity and arrogance, however slightly they may manifest themselves, nevertheless weaken the guarding of the entrance, they are gaps in the gatekeeper's character. Added to this is the fact that the gatekeeper seems to have a friendly disposition by nature, he is certainly not always an official. In the very first moments he makes the joke of inviting the man to enter despite the prohibition which he expressly maintains, then he does not send him away, but gives him, as it says, a stool and allows him to sit down to one side of the door. The patience with which he endures the man's requests through all the years, the little interrogations, the acceptance of gifts, the graciousness with which he allows the man beside him to curse loudly the unfortunate chance that placed the gatekeeper here — all this suggests stirrings of compassion. Not every gatekeeper would have acted like this. And finally, at a mere beckoning, he bends down low over the man to give him an opportunity for the last question. Only a faint impatience — the gatekeeper knows, after all, that everything is over — is expressed in the words: ‘You are insatiable.’ Some go even further in this kind of interpretation and think that the words ‘You are insatiable’ express a kind of friendly admiration, though admittedly not free from condescension. In any case, this rounds out the figure of the gatekeeper differently from what you believe.” “You know the story more thoroughly than I do and have known it longer,” said K. They were silent for a little while. Then K. said: “So you believe the man was not deceived?” “Do not misunderstand me,” said the priest, “I am merely showing you the opinions that exist about it. You must not pay too much attention to opinions. The text is unchangeable and opinions are often only an expression of despair at that. In this case there is even an opinion according to which it is precisely the gatekeeper who is deceived.” “That's a far-reaching opinion,” said K. “How is it supported?” “The argument,” answered the priest, “starts from the gatekeeper's simple-mindedness. It is said that he does not know the interior of the Law, but only the path which he must walk up and down before the entrance. His ideas about the interior are thought to be childish, and it is assumed that he himself fears what he wants to make the man afraid of. Indeed, he fears it more than the man, for the man wants nothing other than to enter, even after he has heard about the terrible gatekeepers inside, whereas the gatekeeper does not want to enter, at least we are told nothing about it. Others do say that he must already have been inside, for at some point he was taken into the service of the Law, and that could only have happened inside. To this one must reply that he might well also have been appointed gatekeeper by a call from inside, and that at least he can hardly have been far inside, since he cannot bear the sight of even the third gatekeeper. Moreover, it is not reported that in all those years, apart from his remark about the gatekeepers, he told anything at all of the interior. It might be forbidden to him, but he has told nothing of the prohibition either. From all this it is concluded that he knows nothing of the appearance and significance of the interior, and is deceived about it. But he is also supposed to be deceived about the man from the country, for he is subordinate to this man and does not know it. That he treats the man as a subordinate can be seen from many things you probably still remember. But that he is actually subordinate to him is said, according to this opinion, to emerge just as clearly. Above all, the free man is superior to the bound one. Now the man is in fact free, he can go wherever he wants, only entry into the Law is forbidden him, and that only by a single person, the gatekeeper. If he sits down on the stool to one side of the gate and remains there all his life, he does so voluntarily, the story tells of no compulsion. The gatekeeper, on the other hand, is bound to his post by his office, he may not go away outside, but to all appearances he may not go inside either, even if he wanted to. Moreover, although he is in the service of the Law, he serves only at this entrance, and therefore only for this man, for whom alone this entrance is intended. For this reason too he is subordinate to him. It must be assumed that for many years, for the whole length of a man's life, as it were, he has performed only empty service, for it is said that a man comes, that is, a grown man, so that the gatekeeper had to wait a long time before his purpose was fulfilled, and had to wait as long as it pleased the man, who came voluntarily, after all. But the end of his service too is determined by the end of the man's life, so until the end he remains subordinate to him. And again and again it is emphasised that the gatekeeper seems to know nothing of all this. But nothing remarkable is seen in that, for according to this opinion the gatekeeper is labouring under a much graver deception still, and it concerns his service. At the end, namely, he speaks of the entrance and says: ‘I am going now to close it,’ but at the beginning it says that the gate to the Law stands open as it always does, and if it always stands open, always, that is, independently of the lifetime of the man for whom it is intended, then even the gatekeeper will not be able to close it. Opinions differ as to whether, in announcing that he will close the gate, the gatekeeper wants merely to give an answer, or to emphasise his official duty, or to plunge the man into regret and grief at the very last moment. But many agree that he will not be able to close the gate. They even believe that, at least at the end, he is subordinate to the man in knowledge too, for the man sees the radiance streaming from the entrance to the Law, while the gatekeeper, as such, presumably stands with his back to the entrance, nor does any remark of his show that he has noticed a change.” “That's well supported,” said K., who had repeated individual passages from the priest's explanation to himself under his breath. “It's well supported, and now I too believe that the gatekeeper is deceived. But that hasn't made me abandon my earlier opinion, for the two partly coincide. It makes no difference whether the gatekeeper sees clearly or is deceived. I said the man is deceived. If the gatekeeper sees clearly, one could doubt that, but if the gatekeeper is deceived, then his deception must necessarily be passed on to the man. In that case the gatekeeper is admittedly not a fraud, but so simple-minded that he ought to be driven out of the service at once. You must consider, after all, that the deception under which the gatekeeper labours does him no harm, but harms the man a thousandfold.” “Here you come up against an opposing opinion,” said the priest. “For some say that the story gives no one the right to judge the gatekeeper. However he may appear to us, he is nevertheless a servant of the Law, and thus belongs to the Law, and thus is removed from human judgement. In that case one must not believe that the gatekeeper is subordinate to the man either. To be bound by one's service even merely to the entrance to the Law is incomparably more than to live freely in the world. The man only approaches the Law, the gatekeeper is already there. He is appointed to his service by the Law, to doubt his worthiness would mean doubting the Law.” “I don't agree with that opinion,” said K., shaking his head, “for if one accepts it, one has to take everything the gatekeeper says as true.
