But you yourself have explained at length why that is impossible.” “No,” said the priest, “one need not take everything as true, one need only take it as necessary.” “A dismal opinion,” said K. “The lie is made into the order of the world.”

K. said this to conclude, but it was not his final judgement. He was too tired to survey all the consequences of the story, and the trains of thought into which it led him were unfamiliar too, unreal things, better suited to discussion among the company of court officials than to him. The simple story had become shapeless, he wanted to shake it off, and the priest, who now showed great tact, allowed it and received K.'s remark in silence, although it certainly did not agree with his own opinion.

They continued walking in silence for a time, K. kept close beside the priest without knowing where he was in the darkness. The lamp in his hand had long since gone out. Once, directly in front of him, the silver statue of a saint flashed with no light but the gleam of the silver, then flickered straight back into the dark. To avoid remaining entirely dependent on the priest, K. asked him: “Aren't we near the main entrance now?” “No,” said the priest, “we are a long way from it. Do you want to leave already?” Although K. had not been thinking of that just then, he said at once: “Certainly, I have to leave. I'm the authorised signatory at a bank, they're waiting for me, I only came here to show a foreign business associate round the cathedral.” “Well,” said the priest, offering K. his hand, “then go.” “But I can't find my way on my own in the dark,” said K. “Go left towards the wall,” said the priest, “then follow the wall without leaving it, and you will find an exit.” The priest had moved only a few steps away, but K. was already calling very loudly: “Please, wait a moment.” “I am waiting,” said the priest. “Isn't there anything else you want from me?” K. asked. “No,” said the priest. “You were so kind to me earlier,” said K., “and explained everything to me, but now you're sending me away as though you didn't care about me.” “But you have to leave,” said the priest. “Yes,” said K., “do understand that.” “First understand who I am,” said the priest. “You're the prison chaplain,” said K., moving closer to the priest, his immediate return to the bank was not as necessary as he had made out, he could perfectly well remain here a while longer. “So I belong to the court,” said the priest. “Why, then, should I want anything from you. The court wants nothing from you. It receives you when you come, and it releases you when you go.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: On the eve of his thirty-first birthday—it was about nine in the evening, the hour when the streets grow quiet—two gentlemen came to K.'s apartment. In frock coats, pale and fat, with top hats that seemed immovably fixed. After a small ceremony at the apartment door over who should enter first, the same ceremony was repeated on a larger scale outside K.'s door. Although no one had announced the visit to him, K. too sat dressed in black, in an armchair near the door, slowly pulling on new gloves that stretched tightly over his fingers, in the manner of someone expecting guests. He got up at once and looked at the gentlemen curiously. “So you're the ones assigned to me?” he asked. The gentlemen nodded; one, holding his top hat, pointed towards the other. K. admitted to himself that he had expected a different visitor. He went to the window and looked once more at the dark street. Almost all the windows on the other side were still dark too, and in many the curtains were drawn. At one lighted window on that floor, little children played together behind a railing, reaching their small hands towards one another, still unable to move from their places. “They send old actors in minor roles for me,” K. told himself, looking round to confirm it once more. “They're trying to finish me off cheaply.” He suddenly turned towards them and asked: “What theatre do you perform at?” “Theatre?” one gentleman asked the other for guidance, the corners of his mouth twitching. The other behaved like a mute struggling with an uncooperative body. “They aren't prepared to be asked questions,” K. told himself, and went to fetch his hat.

The gentlemen wanted to link arms with K. while still on the stairs, but he said: “Not until we're in the street. I'm not ill.” Immediately outside the front door, however, they linked themselves to him in a way he had never walked with another person before. They held their shoulders close behind his, and instead of bending their arms, used them to entwine K.'s arms along their full length; at the bottom they grasped his hands with a textbook, practised, irresistible grip. K. walked rigidly upright between them. The three now formed such a single unit that if one of them had been smashed, all would have been smashed. It was a unity almost only lifeless things can form.

Under the street lamps K. repeatedly tried, difficult though it was with them pressed so close together, to see his companions more clearly than had been possible in the half-light of his room. Perhaps they're tenors, he thought at the sight of their heavy double chins. The cleanliness of their faces disgusted him. One could almost still see the cleansing hand that had probed the corners of their eyes, rubbed their upper lips and scraped out the folds of their chins.

When K. noticed this, he stopped, and consequently the others stopped too. They were at the edge of an open, deserted square laid out with ornamental planting. “Why did they send you, of all people?” he exclaimed rather than asked. The gentlemen apparently had no answer. They waited with their free arms hanging down, like attendants when a patient wants to rest. “I'm not going any farther,” K. said experimentally. The gentlemen did not need to answer that; it was enough that they kept their grip tight and tried to lift K. from the spot, but he resisted. “I won't need much strength any more; I'll use it all now,” he thought. He remembered flies straining away from a lime twig, their little legs tearing apart. “The gentlemen will have hard work.”

Then, in front of them, Miss Bürstner came up a little flight of steps from a lower street onto the square. It was not quite certain that it was she, though the resemblance was great. But K. did not care whether it was definitely Miss Bürstner; he merely became conscious at once of the worthlessness of his resistance. There was nothing heroic in resisting, in making difficulties for the gentlemen now, in trying to enjoy the last semblance of life through resistance. He started walking, and some of the pleasure this gave the gentlemen passed back to him. They now allowed him to determine their direction, and he chose the route the young woman was taking ahead of them—not because he wanted to catch up with her, not because he wanted to see her for as long as possible, but merely so as not to forget the admonition she represented for him. “The only thing I can do now,” he told himself, the even rhythm of his steps and those of the other two confirming his thoughts, “the only thing I'm doing now, is to retain to the end a mind that calmly puts things in order. I always wanted to plunge twenty hands into the world, and for a purpose that could not be approved of at that. That was wrong. Am I now to show that not even a year-long trial could teach me anything? Am I to depart as a slow-witted man? Should people be allowed to say that at the beginning of the trial I wanted to end it, and now, at its end, I want to begin it again? I don't want that said. I'm grateful that they've sent these half-mute, uncomprehending gentlemen along with me on this journey, and left it to me to tell myself what is necessary.”

Meanwhile the young woman had turned into a side street, but K. could now do without her and gave himself over to his companions. All three crossed a bridge in the moonlight in complete agreement. The gentlemen now willingly yielded to every small movement K. made; when he turned a little towards the railing, they too turned to face it fully. The water, shining and trembling in the moonlight, divided around a little island on which masses of foliage from trees and shrubs rose in heaps, as though crowded together. Beneath them, now invisible, ran gravel paths with comfortable benches, on which K. had stretched himself in many a summer. “I didn't mean to stop,” he told his companions, embarrassed by their readiness. One seemed to make a gentle reproach to the other behind K.'s back for the mistaken stop, and then they went on.

They passed through several uphill streets where policemen stood or walked here and there, now far away, now very close. One with a bushy moustache, his hand on his sabre hilt, approached the not entirely unsuspicious group as though deliberately. The gentlemen faltered; the policeman seemed already to be opening his mouth when K. forcibly pulled the gentlemen forward. He repeatedly turned round cautiously to see whether the policeman was following, but once they had put a corner between themselves and him, K. began to run, and the gentlemen, despite their great breathlessness, had to run too.

In this way they quickly left the city, which in this direction gave way almost without transition to fields. A small quarry, abandoned and desolate, lay near a house that still looked entirely urban. Here the gentlemen stopped, whether because this place had been their destination from the start or because they were too exhausted to run any farther. Now they let go of K., who waited silently, took off their top hats and wiped the sweat from their foreheads with their handkerchiefs while looking around the quarry. Everywhere the moonlight lay with a naturalness and calm granted to no other light.

After exchanging a few courtesies about who should carry out the next tasks—the gentlemen seemed to have received their instructions without any division of duties—one went to K. and removed his jacket, waistcoat and finally his shirt. K. shivered involuntarily, at which the gentleman gave him a light, reassuring pat on the back. Then he folded the clothes carefully, like things that would be used again, though not in the immediate future. To avoid exposing K. to the rather cool night air without movement, he took him under the arm and walked him up and down a little, while the other gentleman searched the quarry for a suitable spot. When he found it, he beckoned, and the first gentleman led K. over. It was near the quarry face, where a broken-off stone lay. The gentlemen sat K. on the ground, leaned him against the stone and rested his head on top. Despite all their efforts and all the cooperation K. offered, his posture remained very strained and implausible. One gentleman therefore asked the other to leave arranging K. to him alone for a little while, but that made things no better either. Finally they left K. in a position that was not even the best of those they had already achieved. Then one gentleman opened his frock coat and, from a sheath hanging on a belt stretched around his waistcoat, took a long, thin butcher's knife sharpened on both sides, held it up and examined the edges in the light. The repulsive courtesies began again: one passed the knife over K. to the other, who passed it back over K. K. now knew exactly that it would have been his duty to seize the knife himself as it hovered from hand to hand above him and drive it into himself. But he did not do so; instead, he turned his still-free neck and looked around. He could not prove himself entirely, could not spare the authorities all their work. Responsibility for this final failing lay with whoever had denied him the remaining strength needed for it. His eyes fell on the top floor of the house adjoining the quarry. Like a light flaring up, the casements of a window flew apart there, and a person, faint and thin in the distance and height, abruptly leaned far out and stretched their arms still farther. Who was it? A friend? A good person? Someone who cared? Someone who wanted to help? Was it one person? Was it everyone? Was there still help? Were there objections that had been forgotten? There certainly were. Logic is unshakeable, admittedly, but it cannot withstand a person who wants to live. Where was the judge he had never seen? Where was the high court he had never reached? He raised his hands and spread all his fingers.

But one gentleman's hands settled on K.'s throat, while the other thrust the knife into his heart and turned it twice. With his sight failing, K. still saw the gentlemen close before his face, leaning cheek to cheek, watching the outcome. “Like a dog!” he said; it was as though the shame were meant to outlive him.
